This can be done by self-report if the patient is awake and communicative or by using a validated behavioral pain scale [ ] in those who are unable to effectively communicate pain. The use of behavioral pain scales dedicated to non-verbal patients, namely the Behavioral Pain Scale (BPS) and the Critical Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) should be promoted [ , ]. Optimal pain management may be extremely challenging in TBI patients who are often deeply sedated, receive neuromuscular blocking medications (NMB) and may suffer from additional injuries. Medical, nursing and physiotherapy teams should make all the possible efforts to ensure pain management is optimal and avoid extended periods of high-dose intravenous opioid infusions. 6.2.2. B: Both SAT and SBT A spontaneous awakening trial (SAT) is a protocolized pause of intravenous narcotics and sedatives for assessment of level of consciousness. The drugs are restarted at half the prior dose when appropriate. A spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) is a protocolized period of minimal ventilator support, with the goal of assessing ongoing pulmonary ventilator requirements. A randomized, controlled trial comparing daily spontaneous breathing trials (SBTs) to the standard of care in mechanically ventilated patients revealed that those receiving SBTs had a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation (4.5 days vs. 6 days, p = 0.003). There were also fewer ventilator-related complications and lower ICU costs of care in the intervention arm [ ]. Another randomized controlled trial comparing a daily SAT and SBT protocol against daily SBT with routine sedation found that patients on the SAT plus SBT protocol spent more days breathing without assistance and had shorter ICU lengths of stay. Patients receiving daily SAT were also less likely to die during the 12-month follow-up period. Rates of reintubation were similar in the two groups [ ]. Daily consideration of SAT and SBT is a key part of the timely cessation of mechanical ventilation and leads to improved outcomes in the overall critically ill population. Studies comparing approaches specifically in TBI patients are currently lacking. The Extubation strategies in Neuro-Intensive care unit patients and associations with Outcomes (ENIO) international observational study will examine ventilator liberation and tracheostomy practices in such patients [ ]. 6.2.3. C: Choice of Analgesia and Sedation Effective management of pain, anxiety and delirium is an important objective in the ICU, particularly in brain injury patients in whom these symptoms may contribute to increased intracranial pressure. Management should be based on clearly established, patient-oriented goals and standardized assessment measures. There are several validated measures published for assessment of sedation level in the ICU, including the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) and the Riker Sedation-Agitation Scale (RSAS). The most effective medication and titration protocol for sedation and analgesia has yet to be elucidated and may differ depending on the clinical context and patient characteristics. The MENDS randomized, controlled trial compared the benzodiazepine lorazepam and the alpha-2 adrenoreceptor agonist dexmedetomidine for sustained sedation in mechanically ventilated patients and found more days alive without delirium or coma (median 7.0 versus 3.0 days, p=0.01) in the dexmedetomidine arm. Costs of care were similar between the two groups [ ]. The MENDS2 study will compare dexmedetomidine and propofol in septic patients on mechanical ventilation. Results from that study are pending as of the preparation of this manuscript. Studies examining the differential propensity of various sedation regimens to alter the risk of post-traumatic delirium are currently lacking. Patients treated for moderate or severe TBI commonly require pharmacologic sedation for maximal reduction of increased ICP in response to sensory stimulation. Current guidelines recommend the use of barbiturates and/or propofol to control elevated, refractory ICP [ ]. Yet, it has been well recognized that intravenous sedative medications influence the risk for delirium. Sedation with dexmedetomidine significantly reduces the risk for delirium compared to benzodiazepines in mechanically ventilated patients [ , ], and compared to morphine in post-cardiac surgery patients [ ] Dexmedetomidine attenuates sepsis-induced hippocampal microglial activation [ ]. The use of dexmedetomidine as adjuvant sedation to propofol infusion may better reduce neuroinflammatory response because these medications affect neuroinflammation through different mechanisms [ ]. In a mouse model of TBI, treatment with dexmedetomidine attenuates early neurological dysfunction and BBB damage, reduces neutrophil infiltration, microglial activation, and pro-inflammatory mediator secretion, and reduces cellular apoptosis [ ]. Interestingly, a clinical study has shown a significantly lower incidence of delirium after seizures induced by electroconvulsive therapy in patients premedicated with dexmedetomidine [ ]. Although a meta-analysis of nine studies evaluating dexmedetomidine as a sedative and analgesic agent in critically ill adult patients failed to find a statistically significant difference among populations, the prevalence of delirium was lower in the dexmedetomidine group [ , ] and this drug may prove useful

model of TBI, treatment with dexmedetomidine attenuates early neurological dysfunction and BBB damage, reduces neutrophil infiltration, microglial activation, and pro-inflammatory mediator secretion, and reduces cellular apoptosis [ ]. Interestingly, a clinical study has shown a significantly lower incidence of delirium after seizures induced by electroconvulsive therapy in patients premedicated with dexmedetomidine [ ]. Although a meta-analysis of nine studies evaluating dexmedetomidine as a sedative and analgesic agent in critically ill adult patients failed to find a statistically significant difference among populations, the prevalence of delirium was lower in the dexmedetomidine group [ , ] and this drug may prove useful in the prevention of delirium among TBI patients. 6.2.4. D: Delirium: Assess, Prevent and Manage Monitoring for early identification and risk factor modification is a key component of delirium management. As indicated above, the most widely used tool for delirium assessment in the ICU is the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) [ ]. This easy-to-administer bedside tool evaluates patients in four key domains: acute onset of mental status change or fluctuating course, inattention, disorganized thinking and altered level of consciousness. Among seven prospective cohort studies and a total of 1,173 patients, delirium was assessed in neurocritically ill patients using validated delirium tools after considering primary neurologic diagnoses and associated complications, finding a pooled prevalence rate of 12-43%. When able to compare against a common reference standard, Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition, the test characteristics showed a sensitivity of 62-76%, specificity of 74-98%, positive predictive value of 63-91%, negative predictive value of 70-94%, and reliability kappa of 0.64-0.94 [ ]. The Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist (ICDSC) is another widely accepted delirium screening tool [ ]. The ICDSC is comprised of eight items: altered level of consciousness, inattention, hallucination/delusions/psychosis, psychomotor agitation or retardation, inappropriate speech or mood, sleep wake/cycle disturbance and symptom fluctuation. Its pooled sensitivity and specificity in the general ICU population are 74% and 82%, respectively [ ]. Among four studies reporting multivariable analyses, delirium in neurocritically ill patients was associated with increased hospital length of stay (3 studies) and ICU length of stay (1 study), as well as worse functional independence (1 study) and cognition (2 studies), but not survival [ ]. It is important to assess patients regularly to reduce the risk of overlooking hypoactive delirium, regardless of whether they are receiving intravenous sedatives. Spontaneous awakening trials present an optimal opportunity to perform this assessment [ ]. Once hemorrhage, stroke, increased ICP and seizures have been ruled out, management of delirium entails revisiting primary prevention measures, including reorientation, an appropriate sleep environment, and adequate pain management. These interventions are important even in patients whose delirium is in association with sepsis, sedative effect, hypoxia or metabolic compromise. Since the duration of delirium predicts worse long-term cognition and mortality [ ], these nonpharmacologic measures to limit its duration can be expected to improve patient outcomes. 6.2.5. E: Early Mobility and Exercise There is a range of activities from passive range of motion to ambulation with the assistance that can be implemented as part of an early mobility program. Such programs are safe and feasible in critically ill patients and result in fewer days of delirium, shorter duration of mechanical ventilation, shorter ICU length of stay and shorter hospital length of stay. Any member of the care team can perform early mobility activities, although the appropriate level of activity should be determined based on the patient’s level of sedation. Early mobilization during spontaneous awakening trials improved odds of return to independent functional status by discharge (OR 2.7, 95% CI 1.2-6.1) in a series of critically ill adults on mechanical ventilation [ ]. Feasibility of early combined cognitive and physical therapy has also been demonstrated in a similar population [ ] as well as in pediatric TBI patients [ ], and outcomes are currently under study. These findings may be of particular salience in the TBI population given the increased risk for adverse cognitive outcomes compared to the general ICU population. 6.2.6. F: Family Engagement and Empowerment Encouraging family members to participate actively inpatient care can result in improved ICU team performance and communication, reveal important insights to the patient condition and keep providers focused on the most salient goals of care for each patient. Family engagement and empowerment may also lead to early identification of and reduction in the burden of ICU-related psychological and emotional stress among family members (a harbinger of post-intensive care syndrome for the family, or PICS-F) [ ]. Key elements of strategic communication with families include using simplified language, focusing on concrete issues and avoiding the presentation of large boluses of information without adequate time for family members to process. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of protocolized family support interventions found that these interventions reduce ICU length of stay

on the most salient goals of care for each patient. Family engagement and empowerment may also lead to early identification of and reduction in the burden of ICU-related psychological and emotional stress among family members (a harbinger of post-intensive care syndrome for the family, or PICS-F) [ ]. Key elements of strategic communication with families include using simplified language, focusing on concrete issues and avoiding the presentation of large boluses of information without adequate time for family members to process. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis of protocolized family support interventions found that these interventions reduce ICU length of stay but do not adversely affect mortality [ ]. 6.2.7. Implementation Challenges Improvements in compliance with the ICU Liberation bundle are associated with a reduction in mortality and improvement in a number of patient-oriented symptoms including delirium (Fig. 3 ) [ , ]. Yet systematic implementation of this bundle, including delirium screening, is lacking in many ICUs [ - ] due to a number of barriers. Nurses may report that delirium is difficult to evaluate in intubated patients [ , - ] and some feel that sedated patients could not be assessed [ , ]. Importantly, the CAM-ICU was specifically designed to assess nonverbal ICU patients receiving mechanical ventilation, and the current CAM-ICU training manual [ ] indicates that the only condition incompatible with CAM-ICU assessment is unresponsiveness to verbal stimulation (RASS < -3) irrespective of sedative use. Some clinicians suggest that delirium can be identified without an assessment tool [ , ]. Yet without a validated screening tool, nurses and intensivists only recognized 25-35% of delirious days [ , ]. Missed diagnosis may lead to lack of treatment, whereas false positives due to lack of objectivity may expose patients to unnecessary pharmacological therapy despite its unproven efficacy [ ] and safety risks [ , ]. It may be argued that the TBI population represents a unique group of critically ill patients and the focal neurologic deficits in this population may require special delirium evaluation and prevention tools. Indeed, there is limited literature on the best methodologies for implementation of the ICU Liberation bundle, specifically in the trauma ICU population [ ]. Importantly, both the CAM-ICU and the ICDSC have good sensitivity and specificity for evaluating delirium in TBI patients [ , ]. More broadly, the implementation of the ABCDEF Bundle as a whole can substantially improve outcomes, including reducing the odds of developing delirium and reducing the chances of requiring mechanical ventilation in non-ventilated [ , ]. Barriers to implementing the ABCDEF as a bundle are similar to the ones encountered when using a delirium assessment tool. Some are related to the patient, including safety concerns in terms of hemodynamic stability or decreased levels of cooperation [ ]. Other barriers include lack of knowledge about the benefits and efficacy of the bundle, preference for autonomy and perception of increased workload [ - ]. Finally, there are barriers related to the structure of the ICU, including culture and organization, teamwork, physical environment, lack of resources, and inadequate management/leadership [ , , ]. Importantly, implementation of these recommendations can reduce provider workload by optimizing patient interactions and minimizing requirements for ICU-level care. 6.3. Treatment and Prevention of Potential Contributing Factors Optimal treatment of delirium associated with traumatic brain injury is determined by the etiology. Thus, the management necessarily starts with a neurologic assessment to include neurologic examination, brain imaging and consideration of electroencephalography (EEG). The following subsections describe interventions appropriate for each potential etiology of delirium in this population. 6.3.1. Operative Management of Intracranial Hemorrhages Patients with hemorrhages evident on brain computed tomography (CT) imaging may benefit from surgical intervention, and recommendations vary depending on the brain compartment in which the hemorrhage occurs. Evacuation is recommended for epidural hematomas (EDH) greater than 30cm 3 and for EDH with extenuating factors (GCS less than 9, clot thickness greater than 15mm, midline shift greater than 5mm or focal neurological deficits) [ ]. Patients should be considered for the evacuation of subdural hematomas (SDH) that are larger than 1 cm or associated with midline shift greater than 5 mm, a rapidly declining GCS, GCS less than 9, asymmetric or fixed and dilated pupils, or intracranial pressure (ICP) > 20 mmHg [ ]. A randomized controlled trial of early surgical evacuation in patients with traumatic intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) greater than 10mL, 2/3 of whom had GCS between 9 and 14, found improved 6-month mortality in the surgical group. Effects on delirium were not reported [ ]. 6.3.2. Intracranial Pressure Management 6.3.2.1. Monitoring Patients with severe TBI (indicated by a Glasgow Coma Score of 8 or less and abnormalities on CT scan) should be considered for intracranial pressure monitoring once the patient’s airway and hemodynamic stability have been addressed. This may be accomplished using intraparenchymal monitors (placed

pressure (ICP) > 20 mmHg [ ]. A randomized controlled trial of early surgical evacuation in patients with traumatic intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) greater than 10mL, 2/3 of whom had GCS between 9 and 14, found improved 6-month mortality in the surgical group. Effects on delirium were not reported [ ]. 6.3.2. Intracranial Pressure Management 6.3.2.1. Monitoring Patients with severe TBI (indicated by a Glasgow Coma Score of 8 or less and abnormalities on CT scan) should be considered for intracranial pressure monitoring once the patient’s airway and hemodynamic stability have been addressed. This may be accomplished using intraparenchymal monitors (placed directly into brain tissue) or by placement of an extraventricular drain (EVD) connected to an external pressure transducer or fiber optic catheter, allowing for therapeutic ventricular drainage while performing continuous intracranial pressure monitoring [ ]. The EVD and fiber optic cable have the benefit of providing a method of lowering ICP by continuous or intermittent CSF drainage. The target ICP is less than or equal to 20 mmHg, with a corresponding cerebral perfusion pressure (estimated as the difference between mean arterial pressure and ICP) of 50-70 mmHg. In a retrospective matched cohort study of patients in the Brain Trauma Research Center (BTRC) database, continuous drainage was associated with, on average 5.7 mmHg lower pressures and significantly lower burden of intracranial hypertension (ICP > 20 mmHg) than intermittent drainage [ ]. The continuous drainage approach may increase risk for complications such as catheter clotting, ventriculitis, CSF leak or hemorrhage [ ]. Currently, the intraventricular ICP catheter is considered the most accurate method of ICP monitoring. This design eliminates the need for a fluid-filled system to communicate pressure to an external transducer, thereby significantly reducing the risk of these complications [ ]. Nowadays, the intraventricular ICP catheter is the most accurate monitoring method. This design eliminates the need for a fluid-filled system to communicate pressure to an external transducer, thereby significantly reducing the risk of these complications [ ]. 6.3.2.2. Hypertonic Saline and Mannitol Hypertonic saline and mannitol are the most commonly used agents for the pharmacologic treatment of increased intracranial pressure. Intravascular hyperosmolarity creates an osmolar gradient for water egress from brain parenchyma to the intravascular space, thereby reducing brain volume [ ]. In the case of mannitol, there is also a decrease in blood viscosity and constriction of cerebral conductance vessels, contributing to the reduction of intracerebral blood volume and intracranial pressure [ ]. Based on limited data, there is weak evidence to suggest that hypertonic saline is no better than mannitol in efficacy and safety in the long-term management of acute traumatic brain injury [ ]. Since vasogenic edema sustained by inflammation may prove to be refractory to hyperosmolar therapy, and the principle of only 11% of edema fluid shunted into the blood vessels [ , ] has to be taken under consideration, therapeutic inhibition of inflammation [ - ] and thus of vasogenic edema offers promising perspectives when anti-inflammatory agents are available for clinical studies. 6.3.2.3. Barbiturate Coma Patients with refractory intracranial hypertension in the absence of mass lesions appropriate for surgical intervention can be considered for barbiturate therapy. Pentobarbital suppresses glutamate excitation and prolongs GABA inhibition at the postsynaptic membranes, resulting in a widespread decrease in neuronal activity [ - ]. Treatment with continuous pentobarbital infusion under continuous EEG monitoring can effectively reduce cerebral perfusion pressure, and in on one study resulted in 40% hospital survival rate and 68% rate of good functional outcomes at 1 year after injury [ ]. These benefits must be weighed against the risks to the patient, such as systemic hypotension, hypo- or hyperkalemia and feeding intolerance [ , ]. Hemodynamic stability is essential before and during barbiturate therapy [ ]. Alternative sedative regimens include propofol with morphine or benzodiazepines, although the latter has been associated with an increased risk of delirium [ ]. These sedatives may also decrease systemic blood pressure, resulting reductions in cerebral perfusion pressure, and for this reason ketamine has been proposed as an attractive alternative for maintenance of pharmacologic coma [ ]. Dexmedetomidine has also gained some popularity in the management of refractory intracranial hypertension and shows some promise as an adjunct therapy [ ], although evidence for its routine use in this context is yet to be established. 6.3.2.4. Decompression A randomized clinical trial of bilateral frontotemporoparietal decompressive craniectomy in 155 adult patients with diffuse TBI and refractory ICH (the DECRA Trial) demonstrated lower ICP and shorter ICU lengths of stay with this intervention, however, these results were tempered by diminished long term functional outcomes and lack of improvement in mortality at 6 months after injury [ ]. A second randomized trial in 408 adult and pediatric patients with TBI and refractory ICP (the RESCUEicp Trial) demonstrated lower mortality and disability rates at 6 months after

for its routine use in this context is yet to be established. 6.3.2.4. Decompression A randomized clinical trial of bilateral frontotemporoparietal decompressive craniectomy in 155 adult patients with diffuse TBI and refractory ICH (the DECRA Trial) demonstrated lower ICP and shorter ICU lengths of stay with this intervention, however, these results were tempered by diminished long term functional outcomes and lack of improvement in mortality at 6 months after injury [ ]. A second randomized trial in 408 adult and pediatric patients with TBI and refractory ICP (the RESCUEicp Trial) demonstrated lower mortality and disability rates at 6 months after injury, but higher rates of vegetative state [ ]. The effects of this intervention on delirium associated with TBI have not been directly evaluated. 6.3.2.5. Hypothermia An early systematic review of randomized controlled trials evaluating therapeutic hypothermia in TBI found improved mortality and neurologic function with this intervention [ ]. However, two more recent reviews challenged these findings, raising concerns of risk of bias and quality of evidence [ , ]. The multicenter Prophylactic Hypothermia Trial to Lessen Traumatic Brain Injury-Randomized Controlled Trial (POLAR-RCT) compared 266 patients on prophylactic hypothermia to 245 patients with normothermic management and found substantially similar 6-month neurologic and functional outcomes in the two groups [ ]. 6.3.3. Seizure Management In patients with serious head trauma, seizure prophylaxis with phenytoin (a voltage-dependent sodium channel antagonist [ ]) or levetiracetam (an N-type calcium channel inhibitor that exerts its effects through modulation of the synaptic vesicle-2A protein [ , ]) decreases the risk of early posttraumatic seizures and is recommended during the first 7 days [ , ]. Given that nonconvulsive seizures commonly present with signs of delirium such as confusion, inattention and fluctuations in mental status, a low threshold should be maintained for considering EEG monitoring in patients with TBI and delirium. The Brain Trauma Foundation and the Guidelines for the Management of Severe Traumatic Brain Injury, Fourth Edition [ ] do not suggest routine continuous EEG monitoring in TBI patients, focusing instead on ICP, CPP and blood pressure management [ ]. Nonetheless, seizures are frequently associated with TBI. Posttraumatic seizures occur in 21–27% of moderate to severe TBI patients and are generally associated with haemorrhagic lesions of the temporal lobe [ - ]. The first event of recorded seizures typically occurs during the first 24 hours after TBI, with over one-third being nonconvulsive in nature [ ]. TBI-related seizures can also be induced by increased ICP, cerebral metabolic crisis associated with disturbances in oxidative metabolism and glucose consumption, and impaired redox state of the brain [ ]. A prospective cohort study of continuous EEG in 50 inpatients greater than 65 years of age with delirium found 12% in non-convulsive status epilepticus. Thirty percent of participants had epileptiform activity on EEG, suggesting the delirium was caused by intermittent seizures [ ]. In a retrospective cohort of older adults with delirium who received EEG in the emergency room, epileptiform activity was found in 15% [ ]. Seizures may be a significant risk factor for post-TBI delirium. Continuous electroencephalography may improve the detection of seizures, particularly those that are non-convulsive in nature, and should be considered among the guidelines for the management of traumatic brain injury. Convulsive or nonconvulsive seizures that are refractory to standard prophylactic doses of antiepileptic medications should prompt consideration of dose escalation and neurological consultation. The first-line therapy for status epilepticus in this context is a fast-acting benzodiazepine such as lorazepam or midazolam, to be given intravenously. Accepted second-line therapies include intravenous phenytoin, fosphenytoin (a phenytoin pro-drug with lower risk of cardiac and subcutaneous adverse effects [ ]), valproate [ ] or levetiracetam [ , ]. Pharmacologic coma, e.g . with propofol, barbiturates or ketamine, is an accepted therapy for refractory status epilepticus [ ]. Ketamine is novel among the drugs typically used to control seizures due to its use-dependent blockade of excitatory synaptic activity via modulation of the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor [ ]. Status epilepticus that persists or recurs despite anesthetic coma is termed “super-refractory” [ ]. A number of novel neurotherapies have been investigated for this clinical scenario. For example, allopregnanolone, a positive modulator of synaptic and extrasynaptic GABA type A receptors, showed success in small case series [ , ], but a phase III clinical trial of brexanolone (a proprietary formulation of the same drug) in 132 patients at 122 sites around the world failed to show a benefit over placebo infusion [ ]. 6.3.4. Management of Post-Intensive Care Syndrome All critical care survivors are at risk for Post Intensive Care Syndrome (PICS), a potentially crippling combination of physical, psychological and cognitive sequelae of critical illness and ICU care [ - ]. The psychological impacts of PICS can affect family members and caregivers of critically ill patients as well [ ]. Delirium

success in small case series [ , ], but a phase III clinical trial of brexanolone (a proprietary formulation of the same drug) in 132 patients at 122 sites around the world failed to show a benefit over placebo infusion [ ]. 6.3.4. Management of Post-Intensive Care Syndrome All critical care survivors are at risk for Post Intensive Care Syndrome (PICS), a potentially crippling combination of physical, psychological and cognitive sequelae of critical illness and ICU care [ - ]. The psychological impacts of PICS can affect family members and caregivers of critically ill patients as well [ ]. Delirium in the ICU increases risk for PICS [ ], and TBI patients and their families may be at even higher risk because of the neurologic compromise intrinsic to their injury [ ]. Patients and their families should be evaluated for PICS and those having signs and symptoms of this disorder should be managed by a multidisciplinary team including intensivists, neuropsychiatrists, respiratory and physical therapists, and with the consideration of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions as appropriate [ , ]. 7. FUTURE DIRECTIONS Further investigation of the unique problems, pathophysiology and pharmacologic needs of ICU delirium in TBI is desperately needed to reduce the burden of disease in patients with moderate to severe TBI. This will depend on elucidation of the neuropathological and neurophysiological characteristics of each etiologic contributor independently and when they occur in concert, and on further elucidation of the mechanistic pathways by which these contributors lead to delirium in TBI patients. It will also require a detailed epidemiologic and clinical understanding of the presentations of delirium in TBI patients, and further evaluation of the efficacy of delirium interventions in this population. A significant decrease in TBI-induced biochemical injury seems to be a promising option for delirium prevention or treatment. Hence, further systematic clinical study should be performed to confirm the experimentally documented neuroprotective and neuroregenerative effects of individual medications and medication classes, especially flavonoids as described above, in treatment and prevention of delirium in TBI patients, and of the effects of these medications on long term recovery and cognition. CONCLUSION Delirium in patients admitted to the ICU after traumatic brain injury is very common, occurring in 50-75% of patients. The changes persist in up to 70% of patients with TBI who suffer from delirium upon arrival to inpatient neurorehabilitation. Delirium is a devastating form of brain dysfunction linked to increased mortality, prolonged hospital stay, increased financial cost and long-term cognitive impairment in the TBI population. Therefore, all ICU patients must be actively monitored for the presence of delirium during their entire hospital stay. The etiology of delirium is not fully elucidated but known to be multifactorial. Both focal or diffuse brain dysfunction due to the primary injury as well as secondary brain injuries such as due to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) from hemorrhage or edematous states multiple subjects in TBI patients. However, other etiologies occurring in all ICU patients are also common, including adverse effects of intravenous sedatives or other centrally acting drugs, organ failure leading to metabolic disequilibrium or systemic inflammatory response secondary to sepsis. The mechanisms by which these pathways induce or exacerbate delirium are the subject of ongoing inquiry. Optimal treatment of delirium associated with traumatic brain injury is determined by the etiology. Attention must be paid to adequate pain control, avoidance of oversedation and providing early mobility adequate to patient functional status after TBI. For decades, nonpharmacologic interventions have been the cornerstone of delirium management and treatment. Family involvement and active engagement cannot be overemphasized. To prevent delirium in TBI patients, attention to the ICU environment must be paid to prevent sleep and sensory deprivation, reduce overstimulation and psychological stress.

chunks.content: Introduction SARS-CoV-2 infection has been shown to induce generation of multiple types of autoantibodies and autoimmune diseases – . The variety of tissues damaged by autoimmune reactions during SARS-CoV-2 infection has not yet been satisfactorily explained. Cross-reactivity of antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 S protein to human tissue antigens is one of the possible mechanisms for multi-system disorders. Vojdani et al. have indicated that the potential for cross-reactivity of antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 is substantial , . Antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 had reactions with a wide range of different human tissue antigens, among which there are myelin basic protein, collagen, thyroid peroxidase, transglutaminase 3, transglutaminase 2, α-myosin and others , . As follows from the above works, monoclonal antibodies are usually used to study the cross-binding of anti-S protein antibodies to body proteins , . It is not known whether cross-reactivity is realized in an organism where the immune response against S protein is polyclonal. In addition to anti-SARS-CoV-2 S protein antibodies that cross-react to autoantigens, autoantibodies and autoreactive lymphocytes specific to angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) may be equally important factors in a variety of autoimmune manifestations in COVID-19. Autoantibodies and lymphocytes against ACE2 can be induced in the course of SARS-CoV-2 infection through idiotype-antiidiotypic interactions with lymphocytes against S protein receptor-binding domain. Many patients with a history of SARS-CoV-2 infection have autoantibodies specific for ACE2 , , . Expression of ACE2 was found in many cells and tissues including vascular endothelia, kidney tubular epithelium, intestinal epithelial cells of the gut, cardiovascular tissues, testes, ovary and breast – . Ubiquitous of ACE2 within the human body is the reason to consider autoimmunity to ACE2 as the main factor of damage to many tissues during SARS-CoV-2 infection. Here, we aimed to determine whether ACE2-expressing cells are damaged in response to SARS-CoV-2 S protein immunization. It has been shown that S protein from various SARS-CoV-2 variants (Alpha, Delta and Omicron) binds to rat ACE2 . This allows rats to be considered a suitable model for studying the autoimmune reactions to ACE2, triggered by SARS-CoV-2 S protein. Materials and methods Rats Outbred Wistar rats of both sexes (8–10 weeks old, body weight 198 ± 15 g) were obtained from the Rappolovo breeding facility (Rappolovo, Russia). Animal experiments were performed in accordance with the ARRIVE guidelines, the U.K. Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act, 1986, and EU Directive 2010/63/EU for animal experiments. For all the procedures, we sedated the rats using conventional formulation of Xylazine (Xylanit, NITA-FARM, Saratov, Russia), (10 mg/kg body weight, subcutaneously). At the end of the study, rats were euthanized using a 50% volume per minute displacement rate of carbon dioxide for 2 min. Exposure times of at least 11 min in 100% carbon dioxide were required to ensure irreversible euthanasia of rats. Food and water refusal, loss of more than 15% of body weight over two days, convulsive breathing and breathlessness were considered as humane end-point criterion. No rats reached the above criteria; therefore, all animals were euthanized based on the predetermined time-point (10 weeks after immunization). All procedures were performed by veterinary staff. The protocol and procedures employed were ethically reviewed and approved by the Bioethics Committee of Udmurt State University (Date January 20, 2022/ No. 2201). All methods reported in this study were conducted in compliance with relevant ethical guidelines and regulatory standards. Detection of SARS-CoV-2 in Wistar rat tissues RNA extraction from rat lung, kidney and spleen was carried out using the RNA extraction kit RealBest Sorbitus (Vector-Best, Koltsovo, Russia) as per manufacturer’s instructions. Real-time RT‐PCR technique was used to verify the presence of SARS‐CoV‐2 RNA. PCR was performed with SARS-CoV-2 RNA reverse transcription kit (Vector-Best, Koltsovo, Russia). Immunization Wistar rats (5 males and 5 females) were immunized with 200 μl emulsion, containing 18 μg of SARS-CoV-2 S protein (ACROBiosystems Inc., Newark, USA) and 100 μl incomplete Freund’s adjuvant (IFA) intradermally. Control group of Wistar rats (4 males and 3 females) were injected with 200 μl saline/IFA. After immunization the rats were monitored daily. The rats were sacrificed 10 weeks after immunization. Histological analysis of lungs and kidneys Tissues were fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin for 24 h without inflation and embedded in paraffin. The paraffine sections of kidneys and lungs were cut into slices of 5‑µm thickness and mounted on glass slides. The sections were dewaxed at 40 °C, immersed in two changes of xylene, and then rehydrated in a graded ethanol series. The lungs sections were stained with hematoxylin–eosin and the kidney sections were stained with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) reaction (Biovitrum, Saint-Petersburg, Russia). After coloring, all sections were carried out using alcohols of ascending concentration, soaked in xylene, enclosed in BioMount (Bio Optica Milano Spa, Italia) and studied under a light microscope. All the sections were viewed and assessed blindly by three independent investigators. The pathological changes in the kidneys

cut into slices of 5‑µm thickness and mounted on glass slides. The sections were dewaxed at 40 °C, immersed in two changes of xylene, and then rehydrated in a graded ethanol series. The lungs sections were stained with hematoxylin–eosin and the kidney sections were stained with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) reaction (Biovitrum, Saint-Petersburg, Russia). After coloring, all sections were carried out using alcohols of ascending concentration, soaked in xylene, enclosed in BioMount (Bio Optica Milano Spa, Italia) and studied under a light microscope. All the sections were viewed and assessed blindly by three independent investigators. The pathological changes in the kidneys were assessed by tubular simplification (absence or thinning of brush border of the proximal tubules, destruction of epithelium, dilation of proximal tubules lumens). The changes were classified on a semiquantitative scale from 0 to 3, depending on the degree of proximal tubules involvement: 0—normal; 1—mild—involvement by 10–25%; 2—moderate—involvement by 25–50%; 3—severe—involvement > 50%. Analysis of lymphocytic infiltration of kidneys and lungs The paraffin sections of kidneys and lungs were dewaxed and rehydrated according to the standard procedure described in “ ” section. The sections were autoclaved at 120 °C in a sodium citrate buffer (pH 6.0) for 10 min for antigen retrieval. The tissues were then incubated in 1% hydrogen peroxide for 15 min, washed in PBS/Tween 20 and blocked with 1% bovine serum albumin in PBS/Tween 20 at room temperature (RT) for 1 h. Then, the sections were incubated with the primary antibodies for 1 h at RT, followed by incubation with the secondary antibodies for 1 h at RT. The primary antibodies used in the present study included mouse monoclonal antibodies to rat CD3 (Elabscience Bionovation Inc., Houston, USA), rabbit polyclonal antibodies to CD4 (Affinity Biosciences Ltd., Cincinnati, USA), rabbit polyclonal antibodies to CD8 (Affinity Biosciences Ltd., Cincinnati, USA), and mouse monoclonal CD45RA antibodies (Elabscience Bionovation Inc., Houston, USA). HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG, IgM, IgA antibodies and goat anti-rabbit IgG, IgM, IgA antibodies (IMTEK Ltd., Moscow, Russia) were used as secondary antibodies. Both primary and secondary antibodies were diluted in PBS/Tween 20 containing 1% BSA. The conjugate’s peroxidase label was visualized by DAB (DAB Substrate Kit, Abcam Ltd., Cambridge, USA). Immunostaining was contrasted with hematoxylin. The sections were dehydrated in a graded ethanol series, immersed sequentially in two changes of xylene and mounted with a coverslip. Immunohistochemical staining of lungs for ACE2, surfactant associated protein C and aquaporine 5 Sections of the lungs were prepared and stained by the method described in “ ” section. Type 1 pneumocytes were identified using rabbit polyclonal antibodies to AQP5 (Affinity Biosciences Ltd., Cincinnati, USA). Type 2 pneumocytes were stained with rabbit polyclonal antibodies to ACE2 (Affinity Biosciences Ltd., Cincinnati, USA) or rabbit polyclonal antibodies to SP-C (Affinity Biosciences Ltd., Cincinnati, USA). To reveal bound antibodies, HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG, IgM, IgA antibodies (IMTEK Ltd., Moscow, Russia) and DAB Substrate Kit (Abcam Ltd., Cambridge, USA) were used. Serum creatinine measurement Creatinine levels were measured in rat blood plasma obtained 10 weeks after S protein immunization using the kinetic Jaffe method, kit Creatinine-Novo-A (Vector-Best, Koltsovo, Russia). The working solution, containing picric acid (21.7 mmol/L), sodium tetraborate (20 mmol/L), and sodium hydroxide (0.192 mol/L), was preheated to 37 °C. Then, 100 μL of either the test serum sample or the calibration sample (a creatinine solution with a concentration of 240 μmol/L in hydrochloric acid) was added to 1000 μL of the working solution. The mixture was thoroughly mixed, and after 30 s of incubation, the absorbance was read at 500 nm against water. The measurement was repeated after 60 s. The concentration of creatinine (C) in the blood serum was calculated as follows: C, μmol/L = (∆E/∆Ek) × Ck, where ΔE is the difference in optical densities between the first and second measurements of the test sample; ΔEk is the difference in optical densities between the first and second measurements of the calibration sample; Ck is the creatinine concentration in the calibration sample (μmol/L). ELISA of antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 S protein and autoantibodies to ACE2 Sera of the rats, immunized with SARS-CoV-2 S protein were tested for antibodies to S protein, autoantibodies to ACE2. Antibodies were determined weekly for 10 weeks. To determine anti-S protein antibodies, we used plates coated with recombinant SARS-CoV-2 S glycoprotein (full-sized trimerized surface glycoprotein S, including a receptor-binding domain—RBD) (Vector-Best, Koltsovo, Russia). Serum samples were added in a 1:400 dilution with PBS/Tween 20. After 30-min incubation at 37 °C and subsequent washing of the wells with PBS/Tween 20, 100 µl of antibodies to rat immunoglobulins conjugated to horseradish peroxidase were added to the wells (IMTEK Ltd., Russia). Then, the substrate mixture (5 ml citrate buffer solution [pH 5.0]/3 mg ortho-phenylenediamine/15 ml 3% H 2 O 2 ) was added. Absorbances were read after 15 min at 492 nm. For

protein antibodies, we used plates coated with recombinant SARS-CoV-2 S glycoprotein (full-sized trimerized surface glycoprotein S, including a receptor-binding domain—RBD) (Vector-Best, Koltsovo, Russia). Serum samples were added in a 1:400 dilution with PBS/Tween 20. After 30-min incubation at 37 °C and subsequent washing of the wells with PBS/Tween 20, 100 µl of antibodies to rat immunoglobulins conjugated to horseradish peroxidase were added to the wells (IMTEK Ltd., Russia). Then, the substrate mixture (5 ml citrate buffer solution [pH 5.0]/3 mg ortho-phenylenediamine/15 ml 3% H 2 O 2 ) was added. Absorbances were read after 15 min at 492 nm. For the detection of autoantibodies to ACE2, plates (Corning-Costar, Acton, MA, USA) were coated overnight at 4 °C with ACE2 (ProSpec-Tany TechnoGene Ltd., Rehovot, Israel) 10 μg/mL in PBS, pH 7.4. Plates were blocked with 150 μl of 0.15 mol/l PBS/0.05%BSA/Tween 20. Serum samples were added in a 1:100 dilution in PBS/Tween 20 and incubated for 1 h at RT. The plates were then incubated for 1 h at RT with 100 μl of goat anti-rat Ig (IgG, IgM, IgA) conjugated to horseradish peroxidase (IMTEK Ltd., Moscow, Russia). Then, the substrate mixture (5 ml citrate buffer solution [pH 5.0]/3 mg ortho-phenylenediamine/15 ml 3% H 2 O 2 ) was added. Absorbances were read after 15 min at 492 nm. Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism Software. Shapiro–Wilk test for testing the normality of data was used. Statistical significance between groups was determined by t test. P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Autoantibodies against ACE2 in rats immunized with SARS-CoV-2 S protein Immunization with SARS-CoV-2 S protein caused the production of autoantibodies to ACE2 in 70% rats (Fig. , Table ). The production of autoantibodies to ACE2 reached its maximum level in the blood after 2 weeks, whereas the maximum level of autoantibodies to S protein was observed 3–4 weeks after immunization with S protein (Fig. ). The phenomenon of the production of antiidiotypic autoantibodies (including anti-idiotypic autoantibodies induced by a viral protein) ahead of idiotypic antibodies to an immunogen was observed by us earlier and described by other researchers , . The level of antibodies to S protein and the level of autoantibodies to ACE2 vary reciprocally (Fig. ), which is a characteristic feature of the kinetics of antibodies bound in idiotype-antiidiotypic interactions. Viral RNA in tissues The Wistar strain belongs to the species Rattus norvegicus, which has been shown to be susceptible to infection with Alpha, Delta, and Omicron variants . Therefore, Wistar rats can be carriers of SARS-CoV-2. In the tissues of Wistar rats used in the present experiment, SARS‐CoV‐2 RNA has not been detected. Kidneys In the kidneys of rats immunized with S protein, thinning or loss of brush border of the proximal tubules, destruction of epithelial cells and focal ruptures of tubular basement membrane of the proximal tubules were found (Fig. a,c). The tubular lumen of proximal tubules was dilated (Fig. a,c). Alterations/loss of brush border was revealed in 100% rats immunized with S protein (Table ). The intensity of the damage varied from local to total, when the brush border was damaged in most of the proximal tubules (Fig. e). In some animals, the enlargement of Bowman space was revealed (Fig. a,c). No kidney changes were found in the control group that received the IFA injection. It is known that ACE2 is expressed in the apical brush borders of the proximal tubule epithelial cells as well as the podocytes in less intensity . Inasmuch ACE2 is expressed in the brush border of the proximal cells, it is considered that these cells are susceptible to direct injury caused by SARS-CoV-2 infection , , . We found damage to the brush border in response to immunization with SARS-CoV-2 S protein in the absence of SARS-CoV-2 infection. There was no connection between the presence of autoantibodies to ACE2 in the blood and damage to the proximal renal tubules. However, CD3 + , CD4 + and CD8 + lymphocytic infiltration in the renal cortical interstitium was found in rats with damaged proximal tubules (Fig. ). Consequently, damage to the epithelial cells of the proximal renal tubules expressing ACE2 may be mediated by autoreactive T cell response. The creatinine level measured in rat sera 10 weeks after immunization with SARS-CoV-2 S protein varies extremely (Table ). However, no significant changes in creatinine level in S protein immunized rats relative to the control group receiving IFA were detected ( t test, p ≤ 0.05). Thus, immunization with SARS-CoV-2 S protein caused damage to epithelial cells expressing ACE2 of the proximal renal tubules in rats. Damage to the epithelium of the proximal tubules is associated with their T lymphocytic infiltration. Lungs In 50% of rats immunized with S protein alveolar epithelial hyperplasia was identified (Table , Fig.

cell response. The creatinine level measured in rat sera 10 weeks after immunization with SARS-CoV-2 S protein varies extremely (Table ). However, no significant changes in creatinine level in S protein immunized rats relative to the control group receiving IFA were detected ( t test, p ≤ 0.05). Thus, immunization with SARS-CoV-2 S protein caused damage to epithelial cells expressing ACE2 of the proximal renal tubules in rats. Damage to the epithelium of the proximal tubules is associated with their T lymphocytic infiltration. Lungs In 50% of rats immunized with S protein alveolar epithelial hyperplasia was identified (Table , Fig. a,c, Fig. a–c). Mitotic figures (Fig. c) and binucleated cells (Fig. c) can occasionally be found in foci of alveolar epithelial hyperplasia. As it is known, alveolar epithelial hyperplasia is a proliferation of cuboidal type II pneumocytes , . Since type II pneumocytes express ACE2, we expected an increase in the number of ACE2 positive cells in hyperplastic foci. However, only a few cuboidal type II pneumocytes in the focus of hyperplasia were stained with antibodies against ACE2 (Fig. a). The type II pneumocytes have the capacity to transdifferentiate into type I pneumocytes. Within the process of transdifferentiation, type II cells dedifferentiate, proliferate and some of the daughter cells differentiate into type I cells . Jia et al. have shown that the expression of ACE2 in type II pneumocytes positively correlates with the state of cell differentiation. Undifferentiated cells express little ACE2 . We assumed that the unstained cells in hyperplastic foci are type II pneumocytes, undergoing dedifferentiation and proliferation. Staining for surfactant-associated protein C (SP-C), which is known to be type II pneumocyte-specific marker, showed single type II pneumocytes in hyperplastic foci (Fig. a,b). Hyperplastic foci were clearly negative for aquaporin AQP5, which is type I pneumocytes marker (Fig. c), whereas non-hyperplastic areas of the lung in the same section showed strong staining for anti-AQP5 (Fig. d). Thus, hyperplastic foci mainly contain cells, which bear neither type II pneumocytes markers (ACE-2 and SP-C) nor type I pneumocytes marker (AQP5). The morphological analysis of hyperplastic cells showed that they combine features of both type I and type II pneumocytes. These cells exhibited round nuclei and residual lamellar bodies with positive staining for SP-C, features consistent with type II pneumocytes (Fig. b). Unlike type II pneumocytes, the cells exhibited asymmetrically located nuclei and were larger in diameter (12–17 µm) (Fig. b). Moreover, hyperplastic cells had pure cytoplasm similar to type I pneumocytes (Fig. b). Hyperplastic cells in lungs of rats immunized with S protein are likely to be transitional cells, which were described in diverse mouse models of lung injury and in postmortem lung tissue of patients with COVID-19 acute respiratory distress syndrome . Transitional cells refer to type II pneumocytes that have proliferated in an attempt to replace damaged alveolar epithelial cells, but failed to complete trans-differentiation into type I pneumocytes . The transitional state is characterized by markers of cell cycle exit, down-regulation of type 2 pneumocyte markers (ACE-2 and SP-C), absence of type 1 pneumocyte markers, a cuboidal or partially spread morphology, and expression of unique signature genes, including KRT8 . Immunostaining of rat lung sections for CD3, CD4, CD8 and CD45RA revealed the infiltration of CD4 + T lymphocytes and CD45RA + B lymphocytes (Fig. ). Therefore, we cannot rule out that alveolar type II pneumocyte hyperplasia is caused not only by serum autoantibodies to ACE2, but also by antibodies locally produced by infiltrating B cells. In addition to lymphocytic infiltration in lung parenchyma, 2 out of 10 rats immunized with S protein revealed perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and lymphocytic infiltration in the walls of lung vessels (Fig. ). Thus, immunization with SARS-CoV-2 S protein caused alveolar hyperplasia in rats. The foci of hyperplastic alveolar epithelium consist of dedifferentiated type II pneumocyte, contain atypical cells, T and B lymphocytic infiltrates. Discussion Histological analysis of the lungs and kidneys of rats immunized with SARS-CoV-2 S protein revealed hyperplasia and dedifferentiation of type II pneumocytes in the lungs, CD4 + T, CD45RA + lymphocytic infiltration and perivascular lymphocytic infiltration in the lungs, thinning or loss of brush border and destruction of epithelial cells of the proximal renal tubules, CD4 + T and CD8 + T lymphocytic infiltration in areas of proximal tubule damage. We compared the lesions detected in rats with the histopathology detected in COVID-19 patients. Hammoud et al. summarizing 50 articles reporting organ pathology in COVID-19 patients showed that pneumocyte hyperplasia and lymphocyte and/or monocyte infiltrates were found in 60% of cases . The review of articles made by Malik et al. proves that type II pneumocyte hyperplasia is one of the most common shared findings among lung-histological sections of COVID-19 patients . Zeng et al. found perivascular inflammatory infiltration in the lungs of COVID-19 patient . Patients

T and CD8 + T lymphocytic infiltration in areas of proximal tubule damage. We compared the lesions detected in rats with the histopathology detected in COVID-19 patients. Hammoud et al. summarizing 50 articles reporting organ pathology in COVID-19 patients showed that pneumocyte hyperplasia and lymphocyte and/or monocyte infiltrates were found in 60% of cases . The review of articles made by Malik et al. proves that type II pneumocyte hyperplasia is one of the most common shared findings among lung-histological sections of COVID-19 patients . Zeng et al. found perivascular inflammatory infiltration in the lungs of COVID-19 patient . Patients who died of COVID-19 showed clinical signs of kidney injury that included increased serum creatinine and/or new-onset proteinuria. By light microscopy, proximal acute tubule injury manifested as the loss of brush border, vacuolar degeneration, dilatation of the tubular lumen with cellular debris, and occasionally even frank necrosis and detachment of epithelium with bare tubular basement membrane were noted , . Larsen et al. found damage to the epithelium of the proximal tubules, which included reactive nuclei with mitotic figures and diffuse simplification with the exposure of brush edges in the deceased patient . Consequently, the lesions found in the lungs and kidneys of S protein immunized rats are similar to those found in COVID-19 patients. The mechanism of kidney and lung damage during SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans remains unclear. Viral particles in kidneys were not identified and prominent interstitial inflammation characteristic of many viral nephropathies was not seen in people died from COVID-19 . The RNA of the virus in the kidneys of dead people was also not detected. These facts raise doubts that the cause of tissue damage in SARS-CoV-2 infection is the direct effect of the virus on cells. Induction of SARS-CoV-2 infection-specific damage in rats by S protein immunization without SARS-CoV-2 infection indicates that organ damage is caused by autoimmune reaction induced by viral S protein. Both type II pneumocytes and epithelial cells of the proximal tubules of the kidneys express ACE2. Damage to ACE2 expressing cells in the absence of other obvious damage of the studied organs in rats immunized with S protein indicates that the target of an autoimmune attack induced by S protein immunization is ACE2. Geanes et al. demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 infection can increase autoantibody levels to ACE2 . The levels of these autoantibodies were associated with COVID-19 disease severity , . At the same time, no deposits of immunoglobulins were found in the kidneys . We also found the production of autoantibodies to ACE2 in rats immunized with S protein. Induction of autoreactive lymphocytes to ACE2 may occur via their idiotype–anti-idiotypic interactions with lymphocytes specific to SARS-CoV-2 S protein. Existence of idiotype–anti-idiotypic interactions between autoreactive lymphocytes to ACE2 and lymphocytes to SARS-CoV-2 S protein is likely to take place, as SARS-CoV-2 S protein and ACE2 are complementary . However, no relationship was found between production of autoantibodies to ACE2 and the degree of damage to ACE2 expressing cells. Moreover, in a few rats immunized with S protein, lung and kidney damage occurred in the absence of production of autoantibodies to ACE2. At the same time, infiltration of CD4 + T lymphocytes and CD45RA + B lymphocytes was observed in damaged rat lungs. As is well known, B lymphocytes infiltrating lesion sites may produce disease-specific autoantibodies in some autoimmune diseases . Based on these facts, we assume that the damage of ACE2-expressing cells in the lungs may be caused not only by serum autoantibodies to ACE2 but also by autoantibodies locally produced by infiltrating B cells. The CD4 + T and CD8 + T lymphocyte infiltration observed in the kidneys suggests the key role of anti-idiotypic T cell-mediated autoimmune response against ACE2 in the damage of ACE2-expressing epithelial cells in the kidneys. In human an inflammatory infiltrate was also detected in the interstitial cortex of the kidneys, which consisted of lymphocytes and plasma cells with scattered eosinophils . Not only infection, but also mRNA vaccination with the COVID-19 vaccine can lead to T lymphocytic and macrophage infiltration in the lungs, kidneys, pericardium and myocardium, gastrointestinal tract, bladder and diaphragm, including fatal – . The chronic exposure of a target organ to a complex cytokine mixture, produced by T lymphocytes, could have varying consequences depending on the organ. Target cells could be killed by T lymphocytes. Alternatively, cytokines may alter the normal growth and differentiation of target cells leading to abnormal growth or deficits in cell populations . Conclusion SARS-CoV-2 S protein immunization induces autoimmune reaction attacking ACE2- expressing cells, as a result of which type II pneumocytes undergo hyperplasia and dedifferentiation, epithelial cells of the proximal tubules of the kidneys are destroyed.

chunks.content: Introduction Generic drugs are made to be chemically and therapeutically equivalent to the brand name ones. These equivalencies are obtained at lower costs making generic drugs use certainly appealing. Therefore, many payers/providers have encouraged substitution of brand name drugs with inexpensive bioequivalent generic versions [ ]. In the last 30 years, several controversies concerning generic drugs legislation have arisen. Recent literature reviews demonstrated that physicians, pharmacists and general population hold negative perceptions and knowledge of generic medicines [ - ]. Neuromuscular Blocking Agents (NMBAs) are usually used in patients with altered respiratory mechanics properties such as Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), status asthmaticus or severe acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD) [ , ]. Only few products exhibit the so called ideal Neuromuscular Blockade (NMB) effect which is influenced by several factors namely, required speed of onset and offset, cardiovascular stability, possible accumulation of the NMBA metabolites, elimination routes, and costs [ , ]. One of these products is cisatracurium which is a non-depolarizing NMBA, a benzylisoquinolinium like atracurium, doxacurium, and mivacurium [ ]. Since its introduction in the early 2000, cisatracurium was widely used in Intensive Care Units (ICUs) in developed countries. However, it generated relatively high costs [ ]. Here and there several cisatracurium generics have been developed to respond to the need of lowering expenses. Cisatracurium became of relatively frequent use in critical care, taking advantage of its higher potency and limited side effects [ ]. Payen et al . [ ], reported that NMBAs were used in 9% of patients on day two, 7% on day four and 5% on day six. Cisatracurium accounted for 70% of NMBA use. In developing as in developed countries, cisatracurium use remained rather sporadic [ ]. Recently the introduction of Cisatrex®, the generic of the brand name Nimbex®, provided an opportunity to substitute commonly used NMBAs for cisatracurium. Because of the physicians´ reluctance to prescribe generics due to different controversies, authors hypothesized that a proof of safety and efficacy of Cisatrex® compared to its brand-name could reassure intensivists. The aim of the present study was to compare efficacy and tolerance of two marketed forms, brand-name (Nimbex®) and generic name (Cisatrex®) of cisatracurium-induced paralysis in hypoxemic ventilated patients. Methods Study design and setting: this was a crossover randomized double-blind physiological study conducted in an 8-bed Medical ICU from February 2015 to March 2016, which compared neuromuscular blockade efficacy and tolerance induced respectively by continuous perfusion of brand-name (Nimbex®) and generic name (Cisatrex®) of cisatracurium during two successive time periods. Inclusion criteria: patients admitted to the ICU for severe acute respiratory failure with severe hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 < 200mmHg), presenting important patient-ventilator asynchrony under invasive mechanical ventilation, despite deep analgo-sedation as assessed by Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) [ ], were enrolled when drug induced paralysis was required. Patients with history of allergy to cisatracurium, malignant hyperthermia, pregnancy, neuromuscular disorders or hemodynamic instability, were not included in the present study. Ethics: prior approval of the Local Medical Ethics´ and Research Committee of and written informed consent from family members or surrogates were obtained. Trial registration: isrctn.com ISRCTN89942618. Registered 30 th October 2017. Sample size: it was assessed as the number of patients needed to demonstrate a difference (d) of 10 min in the mean paralysis time delay to reach a defined objective of paralysis assessed by a Train-Of-Four (TOF) ≤2/4. Given, Âµ1= mean delay for Nimbex® to reach TOF=2/4, assessed at 70mn after a trial on a pre-protocol patient. Âµ2= mean delay for Cisatrex® set at 60mn as approximately reported in literature [ ]. d=Âµ1-Âµ2=70-60=10mn. σ=10mn=Standard deviation. Thus, variance is s2=100mn2 (variable distribution was normal and variances were equal). β=0.1 (Thus power of the study is 90%). According to normal distribution: α=5%; Z (1-σ)=1.96; β=10%; Z (1-β)=1.28. The sample size of each group was estimated according to the following formula [ ]: =[((1.96+1.28)2) (102+102)]/102=22 patients in each group. The total sample size (two groups) was estimated at 44 patients. Taking into account the crossover design of the present study the number needed to treat was assessed at 22 patients. Data collection: all data regarding patients´ characteristics at ICU admission, demographic characteristics, underlying diseases, diagnosis at admission, severity of illness, therapeutic characteristics, were collected. Chart abstractors were well trained residents. Before enrollment; clinical, physiological, therapeutic and outcome characteristics were collected at baseline after a short period of respiratory and hemodynamic stabilization. An explicit protocol was used to precise all needed definitions and to ensure uniform handling of collected and measured data. A data form was designed for this purpose. It´s a benzylisoquinolinium used as a neuromuscular-blocking drug similarly to atracurium, doxacurium and mivacurium [ , ]. Nimbex®, the brand name of cisatracurium 2mg/ml, is a trademark of the Glaxo group of companies, AbbVie Corporation licensed use. Active substance: cisatracurium besilate, 6.70mg/1ml or 5mg/1ml expressed in cisatracurium base. Excipients: besilic acid at 32% (qsp pH 3 a 3.8), water for injection. Cisatrex®, 10mg/5ml, producted by MédiS, the generic of cisatracurium. Active substance: cisatracurium besilate 13.4mg (10mg base). Excipients: benzene sulfonic acid 20, water for injection. TOF application device: TOF monitor (Innervator NS252FBB, Fisher-Paykel Health Care, New Zealand) was applied to test twitches of the thumb muscles (number and amplitude) in response to a peripheral neuro-stimulator of the ulnar nerve with a stimulus intensity set at 60mA. Neuromuscular block depth induced by neuromuscular blockade drugs was considered adequate when a target of two responses on the TOF was reached in order to reduce patient-ventilator asynchrony [ , ]. Protocol description: a pre-protocol test was performed on a patient presenting enrollment criteria in order to define the minimum paralysis time delay, recovery time, best intervals for monitoring while training the co-investigator resident (NF) to monitor the different parameters and get familiar with the data collection form. The same co-investigator monitored all included patients to ensure maximal consistency and homogeneity of collected data. After one hour of stabilization period and referring to current state-of-the-art, targeting respiratory and hemodynamic stability, patients were randomized following a double-blind inclusion method, for the two products order of administration, based on a random table. The principal investigator (MB) implemented a random allocation sequence, enrolled and assigned participants to interventions. Table the assigned drug and concealed the sequence until all interventions were performed. Co-investigator (NF), participants and care providers were blinded after assignment to interventions. Minimal patient-ventilator interactions were ensured in all studied patients within the study period. Paralysis depth was monitored by TOF [ ]. A short period of stabilization under effective analgo-sedation as assessed by RSS [ ] was performed. Midazolam and Remifentanyl is the biotherapy, usually used in the ICU, especially in COPD patients. When targeted levels of sedation are not reached, sedation could be switched to propofol and/or fentanyl mainly in ARDS patients. The neuromuscular blockade drug was initiated, continuous infusion of cisatracurium was started at 0.06mg.kg-1.h-1 and increased in increments of 0.03mg.kg-1.h-1 every 30 minutes to reach and sustain a TOF at 2/4, with a maximum study time limited to two hours and a maximum dose of 0.18mg.kg-1.h-1 as assessed by the pre-protocol test patient and The 2002 “Clinical Practice Guidelines for Sustained Neuromuscular Blockade in the Adult Critically Ill Patient” updated in 2016 [ ]. During this same period, the following parameters were measured at equal intervals every five minutes: TOF, heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressures, and ventilatory parameters. The infusion of the first product was stopped after two hours to allow elimination (of the first active paralysis agent) before infusion of the second drug (wash-out period). The one-hour wash-out period was chosen based on the pharmacodynamic properties of the product which suggest that its elimination would be rapid due to its metabolism by Hofmann elimination [ ] and as implied by several studies which assessed a recovery time ranging from 45 min to 68 min [ , - ]. The wash-out period was checked to be quite sufficient to recover a TOF of 4/4 as demonstrated in the pre-protocol test patient. This same period also allowed to monitor the recovery kinetics (recovery time) of the first product. At the end of the wash-out period, the second product was then introduced. Its effect and tolerance (hemodynamic tolerance and drug interaction) were monitored according to the same protocol. Next to the TOF, the monitoring of the paralysis was also assessed by the monitoring of clinical parameters, ventilatory parameters and patient-ventilator asynchronies. Primary outcome: paralysis time delay. It is the time needed from cisatracurium intravenous infusion onset to reach a TOF of 2/4. It was also assessed the respective differences at each time intervals from the cisatracurium intravenous infusion onset until 120 min. Secondary outcomes: recovery time. The time needed to reach a TOF of 4/4 after stopping the cisatracurium intravenous infusion. For commodity reasons, authors rather assessed the respective differences at each time interval from the cisatracurium intravenous infusion cessation until 60 min, especially between the
