Hand-held or pocket echo devices were used by 16% of respondents who were using ultrasounds. Fluid responsiveness was assessed by 835/998 (84%) respondents. Methods used to predict fluid responsiveness are presented in . Cardiac output was measured or monitored by 685/997 (69%) respondents. Methods used to measure or monitor cardiac output are presented in . Venous oxygen saturation was measured by 790/997 (79%) respondents, almost exclusively from a CVC blood sample ( ). Tissue perfusion was assessed biologically (926/997 = 93%) and clinically (624/997 = 63%). Near InfraRed Spectroscopy (NIRS) and video-microscopy were reported to be used by 31/997 (3%) and 9/997 (1%) respondents, respectively. Pulmonary oedema was reported to be detected and quantified using echo (671/998 = 67%), chest X-ray (605/998 = 61%), auscultation (267/998 = 27%) and transpulmonary thermodilution (208/998 = 21%). A comparison between the three main geographical areas (Europe, South America and North America) is presented in . To monitor blood pressure, the first choice was the radial catheter in the three main regions. The femoral catheter was less often used in North America (8%) than in Europe (17%, p < 0.01) or in South America (21%, p < 0.01). To measure cardiac output, ultrasounds were the first choice in the three main regions. Transpulmonary thermodilution was less often used in North America (18%) than in Europe (51%, p < 0.01) or in South America (41%, p < 0.01). To predict fluid responsiveness, ultrasounds were also the first choice in the three main regions, followed by the pulse pressure variation (PPV) and the passive leg-raising (PLR) manoeuvre in comparable proportions. To assess pulmonary oedema, ultrasounds were the first choice in Europe and in South America, and the second choice after chest X-ray in North America. Extravascular lung water measurements were more often used in Europe (29%) and in South America (21%) than in North America (8%, p < 0.01). Discussion Our survey confirms that haemodynamic instability is not uncommon in COVID-19 ICU patients and that different haemodynamicprofiles or phenotypes may be observed with echocardiography. From a monitoring standpoint, SvO 2 was reported to be frequently measured from a CVC, and ultrasounds were reported to be widely used, not only to assess cardiac function but also to predict fluid responsiveness and to assess pulmonary oedema. Therefore, current guidelines regarding the use of echocardiography and the need to predict fluid responsiveness were followed by most respondents. Echocardiographic patterns reported by survey respondents were consistent with cardiovascular clusters recently described in septic shock and underscore the value of ultrasound evaluations to identify the underlying mechanisms of shock and select the most appropriate therapy. Only a minority of echocardiographic evaluations were done using a transesophageal approach. Obesity (frequently reported in COVID-19 patients), mechanical ventilation and prone positioning may render the transthoracic approach challenging. However, the proximity of airways, the risk of aerosol generation and contamination, uncertainties regarding the optimal modalities for probe cleaning, as well as time constraints may have restricted the use of transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Our survey also suggests that hand-held or pocket echo devices were not widely adopted. This may be explained by the fact that these tools are relatively new and that many ICUs have high-end trolley ultrasound machines readily available (e.g. to guide CVC insertion). One factor that may have influenced the importance of ultrasounds in the haemodynamic management of COVID-19 patients is the lack of availability of haemodynamic monitors. Echo evaluations usually take less than 30 min so that, pending proper cleaning, the same device can be used for the haemodynamic assessment of several patients. In contrast, haemodynamic monitors are dedicated to the monitoring of a single patient and are often used several consecutive days. Therefore, the shortage of haemodynamic monitors may have magnified the role of ultrasound techniques in this pandemic context. Another contributing factor is the ability to gather a lot of information from a single echo evaluation. Many respondents used echo not only to assess biventricular function but also to measure cardiac output, to predict fluid responsiveness and to detect lung B lines. Cardiac output was frequently measured (69%). For many respondents ( ), and across the 3 main regions ( ), measurements were performed during echocardiographic evaluations. Otherwise, transpulmonary thermodilution was used by a significant number of respondents, with the exception of North America where uncalibrated pulse contour methods were used more often ( ). This is somewhat surprising given the fact that uncalibrated pulse contour methods are known to have limited accuracy and precision to

Many respondents used echo not only to assess biventricular function but also to measure cardiac output, to predict fluid responsiveness and to detect lung B lines. Cardiac output was frequently measured (69%). For many respondents ( ), and across the 3 main regions ( ), measurements were performed during echocardiographic evaluations. Otherwise, transpulmonary thermodilution was used by a significant number of respondents, with the exception of North America where uncalibrated pulse contour methods were used more often ( ). This is somewhat surprising given the fact that uncalibrated pulse contour methods are known to have limited accuracy and precision to measure cardiac output in septic shock , and their use is not recommended beyond the surgical population . The Swan Ganz catheter was rarely used. Although pulmonary thermodilution remains a monitoring option in patients with septic shock , , this finding is aligned with the global decline of this invasive tool for which the new generation of intensivists did not receive much training. In addition, some clinicians may be reluctant to use a pulmonary artery catheter in the context of hypercoagulability and thromboembolic complications associated with COVID-19 , . The prediction of fluid responsiveness was adopted by a vast majority of respondents (84%). This finding contrasts with the results of a worldwide observational study suggesting that the prediction of fluid responsiveness is not routinely done in ICUs . However, this study done 7 years ago may not reflect current practice anymore. The behaviour of our respondents is supported by recent studies showing outcome benefits when predicting fluid responsiveness in septic patients , . Echo was ranked #1 for the prediction of fluid responsiveness, globally and in the 3 main regions. It was mainly performed with a transthoracic probe (TTE). The prediction of fluid responsiveness with TTE requires the evaluation of the inferior vena cava (IVC) respiratory variations or of the velocity-time integral (VTI) respiratory variations recorded at the level of the left ventricular outflow tract . It is worth noticing that the fully automatic calculation of these variables is not available and that they have a limited sensitivity in patients ventilated with a low tidal volume for protective mechanical ventilation. Indeed, in this context, large IVC or VTI respiratory variations are highly suggestive of fluid responsiveness, but small variations cannot exclude it (false negative). The same limitation applies to PPV and stroke volume variation (SVV) that were also popular methods among our respondents ( ) . The passive leg raising (PLR) manoeuvre is an alternative to TTE-derived variables, PPV and SVV to predict fluid responsiveness during protective mechanical ventilation . It was used by 378 of the 835 respondents (45%) who predicted fluid responsiveness. The use of the PLR manoeuvre requires the simultaneous use of a fast response cardiac output monitoring system (typically a pulse contour technique) in order to capture transient changes in stroke volume or cardiac output during the manoeuvre . Venous oxygen saturation was very frequently measured from a CVC. In sedated patients, the 3 main determinants of venous oxygen saturation are haemoglobin, cardiac output and arterial oxygen saturation. Assuming haemoglobin stability, measuring venous oxygen saturation is a simple way to ensure that fluid restriction and PEEP do not decrease oxygen delivery. Both are used in an attempt to increase arterial oxygenation, but at the same time they are susceptible to decrease cardiac output. Therefore, at least from an oxygen delivery standpoint, the right volume status and the right PEEP level are those associated with the highest venous oxygen saturation . This might be the reason why venous oxygen saturation was so popular among our respondents, but this remains a hypothesis. Indeed, our survey was a snapshot of current behaviours and was not designed to explain these behaviours. The assessment of tissue oxygenation was almost exclusively based on clinical (e.g. capillary refill time) and biological (e.g. kidney function, lactates) evaluations. New techniques such as NIRS and video-microscopy were rarely used. They are probably considered as research tools , and one may imagine they were not available in many ICUs from many countries. Our study has limitations. In addition to emails that are clearly targeted, we used social networks (LinkedIn, Twitter, WhatsApp) to invite clinicians answer the survey and share the link. Therefore, we were not able to control the number of clinicians who received the survey and hence to determine the percentage of respondents. Because the survey was built on a Google platform, it was not accessible from China and we were not able to include the feedback from Chinese doctors who have been involved in the pandemic from the very beginning. However, this is one of the largest surveys ever published in critical care and we have been able to collect almost 900 responses from Europe and America, which are critical areas of the pandemic as

Because the survey was built on a Google platform, it was not accessible from China and we were not able to include the feedback from Chinese doctors who have been involved in the pandemic from the very beginning. However, this is one of the largest surveys ever published in critical care and we have been able to collect almost 900 responses from Europe and America, which are critical areas of the pandemic as well. Finally, this is a survey and not an audit nor an observational study. Therefore, the feedback gathered from clinicians reflects the perception they have of what is done or should be done in their unit, which may sometimes differ from reality . In any case, our results remain of interest to understand where clinicians see value in haemodynamic monitoring tools and practice. Conclusion According to the 1000 intensivists and anaesthetists who sent back a valid questionnaire, vasopressor support was not uncommon in COVID-19 ICU patients. Several haemodynamic phenotypes were reported, highlighting the importance of echocardiography. Ultrasounds were used by many respondents, not only to assess cardiac function but also to predict fluid responsiveness and quantify pulmonary oedema. Venous oxygen saturation measurements from a central venous catheter were also reported to be common practice. Although we observed regional differences, current international guidelines were followed by most respondents. chunks.content: Opioid use disorder (OUD) is a critical comorbidity to assess and manage in people with cancer. Approximately 4% to 7% , of people with cancer have opioid or other substance use disorders, and in certain cancer subtypes (head and neck, esophageal, cervical, and melanoma) the rate of substance use disorders can be as high as 9.74%. Substance use disorders can lead to significant impairment. Indeed, OUD in particular can complicate pain management because opioids are foundational to managing cancer pain. Despite the intersection of cancer and substance use, how best to care for people with cancer and co-occurring OUD is unclear. However, nurses can adapt evidence from the literature and integrate the patient’s goals and social determinants of health to promote well-being. This article discusses safe opioid management in individuals with cancer and OUD, using a composite case example to highlight core approaches, including motivational interviewing, harm reduction, and evidence-based treatments, as well as advocacy for person-centered end-of-life care. Here we focus on the role of the advanced practice nurse (APN), but nurses at any level can use motivational interviewing, incorporate harm-reduction principles, and advocate for evidence-based OUD care. (Although multimodal pain treatment, incorporating both pharmacological and nonpharmacological treatment, is an essential aspect of pain management for people with cancer, it is beyond the scope of this article. For information on adjuvant pain treatments, see “Managing Pain in Critically Ill Adults: A Holistic Approach,” May 2020. ) CARING FOR MR. WRIGHT William Wright, 55, is newly diagnosed with lung cancer with metastases to the spine. He was treated in the hospital for moderate to severe cancer-related pain and plans to initiate first-line cancer-directed treatment. Mr. Wright has a history of untreated OUD (injecting nonmedical fentanyl several times a day). As a first step, nurses caring for a patient like Mr. Wright should use a nonjudgmental approach to explore the substance use history and treatment goals for cancer and OUD. Motivational interviewing techniques can be essential to building rapport, promoting behavioral change, and channeling an individual’s self-efficacy. The key strategies of motivational interviewing include asking open-ended questions, leveraging people’s strengths, using reflective listening, and incorporating summary statements to help patients work through ambivalence to change behavior. Here’s a sample dialogue of how an APN might incorporate these strategies to elicit the patient’s goals regarding opioid use and cancer while assessing the need or readiness for medication treatment: APN: Can you tell me about your opioid use? Mr. Wright: Before my cancer diagnosis, I used fentanyl to unwind after a tough week. But it’s worse lately, and now if I don’t use opioids, I feel sick. APN: It sounds like it has been a difficult time. It takes a lot of courage to reach out to talk to someone. Mr. Wright: I want to treat my cancer and get through it, but I don’t know how I’ll manage without something to take the edge off. The opioids chill me out and help my mind stop racing. APN: It sounds like you have thought about the challenges and benefits of using opioids. Mr. Wright: I have. When I’m using fentanyl, I feel better; but when I stop, then all the things I’ve been avoiding come rushing back. I know I’m risking my health, but I don’t think I can quit on my own. APN: You want to stop using fentanyl, but at the same time it sounds like it helps you manage difficult emotions, pain, and withdrawal symptoms. Do I hear you right? Mr. Wright: Yes, that’s right. APN: Would you be open to trying medication that could assist with the difficult symptoms, such as cravings, pain, and withdrawal, that cause you to use fentanyl? MEDICATION TREATMENT FOR OUD Medication for OUD (MOUD)—specifically, buprenorphine or methadone—is standard treatment for OUD in the context of cancer, ideally in combination with psychosocial support. Buprenorphine , a partial mu-opioid receptor agonist and kappa-opioid receptor antagonist, became available for the treatment of OUD in the office-based setting as part of the Drug Addiction Treatment Act of 2000. Although buprenorphine is a partial agonist, that doesn’t mean it provides only partial analgesia. The analgesia is equivalent to that of full mu-opioid agonists like morphine or fentanyl. But because buprenorphine doesn’t activate the mu-opioid receptor to the same extent as those drugs, the risk of opioid-induced respiratory depression is reduced. Moreover, because buprenorphine has a high affinity for the mu-opioid receptor, it may out-compete and prevent other opioids from binding to and activating the receptor, thus also reducing the risk of opioid-induced respiratory depression caused by other opioids. Initiation of buprenorphine has traditionally required that the person stop taking full opioid agonists (such as morphine or opioids from nonmedical sources) to avoid precipitating withdrawal, but in recent years low-dose methods for starting buprenorphine have emerged in clinical practice. Moderate-to-high-dose

buprenorphine doesn’t activate the mu-opioid receptor to the same extent as those drugs, the risk of opioid-induced respiratory depression is reduced. Moreover, because buprenorphine has a high affinity for the mu-opioid receptor, it may out-compete and prevent other opioids from binding to and activating the receptor, thus also reducing the risk of opioid-induced respiratory depression caused by other opioids. Initiation of buprenorphine has traditionally required that the person stop taking full opioid agonists (such as morphine or opioids from nonmedical sources) to avoid precipitating withdrawal, but in recent years low-dose methods for starting buprenorphine have emerged in clinical practice. Moderate-to-high-dose buprenorphine, administered sublingually and often coformulated with naloxone, can be used to manage cancer pain and OUD. When 16 to 24 mg/day (the typical therapeutic dose for OUD) is administered once a day it manages cravings, but it can be split and administered every six to 12 hours (for example, 8 mg three times a day) to provide analgesia with similar efficacy to that of a traditional full opioid agonist like morphine. , Buprenorphine has the advantage of being both safe and effective for pain and OUD. Additionally, it can be provided outside of specialty OUD care with similar efficacy to and without the potential burdens of methadone, which is required to be dispensed within opioid treatment programs. In January, the Substance Abuse and Mental Heath Services Administration and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced the elimination of the previously required X waiver for buprenorphine prescription. Therefore, any clinician with a current DEA registration to prescribe Schedule III medication can prescribe buprenorphine for OUD. Methadone , a potent mu-opioid agonist, is a highly effective alternative to buprenorphine as a treatment for OUD but may pose logistical and legal challenges for treating concurrent pain and OUD in people with serious illness. Federal law requires individuals treated with methadone for OUD to go to a federal opioid treatment program for regular, often daily, observed dosing.Take-home weekly doses of methadone may be an option for the person in sustained recovery. Methadone has several properties that require consideration, such as drug interactions and the risk of corrected QT interval prolongation, which may cause torsades de pointes. Thus, only clinicians knowledgeable in its management or who have guidance from those with experience with this medication should prescribe it. Like buprenorphine, methadone provides pain relief for only six to 12 hours. Thus, when it is used to treat pain (rather than OUD) more frequent dosing is required, often twice or three times a day. The typical once-a-day dose administered in an opioid treatment program is unlikely to sufficiently control pain, unless the dose is split. Indeed, the methadone dose required to manage OUD (often more than 60 mg/day) is significantly higher than the dose typically required to treat pain. REDUCING HARM Mr. Wright is referred to an outpatient palliative care NP who prescribes sublingual buprenorphine formulated with naloxone 24 mg/day in divided doses (8 mg every eight hours) to address his moderate to severe cancer pain and OUD. He reports less pain and opioid craving, but continues to intermittently use opioids from nonmedical sources. It is common for patients treated with MOUD to continue to use nonprescribed substances, especially in the first months of treatment. Harm reduction is a philosophy and public health construct that focuses on strategies to improve safety, even if there is continued substance use. The concept of harm reduction originated as a means of self-advocacy and management that emphasizes destigmatization, empowerment, and basic human rights. (See , for principles critical to harm reduction.) Incorporating harm reduction is necessary at all points in the substance use continuum, including before, during, and after medical treatment. Nurses at all levels can partner with patients to develop a harm reduction plan. Harm reduction approaches are patient centered (rather than abstinence focused), maximize safety, and encourage engagement in improving health and function. , Patient education is an important aspect of treatment. Mr. Wright should be educated on how MOUD works, its benefits and risks (especially with early discontinuation), and overdose prevention. He should also be informed about the option of additional counseling to address substance use and promote adaptive coping, but this should not be a prerequisite of MOUD treatment. For some nurses, engaging in harm reduction can feel like being complicit in a person’s substance use or encouraging illegal behaviors. However, harm reduction places the person’s well-being at the center of any intervention. Therefore, it is fundamentally aligned with the goals of nursing to facilitate humanization, dignity, choice, quality of life, and healing for persons coping with illness. TREATING PAIN AND OUD Mr. Wright continues 24 mg/day sublingual buprenorphine while following harm reduction recommendations, including carrying naloxone and never using substances when he is alone. Overall, Mr. Wright’s substance use has declined over six months. He says

MOUD treatment. For some nurses, engaging in harm reduction can feel like being complicit in a person’s substance use or encouraging illegal behaviors. However, harm reduction places the person’s well-being at the center of any intervention. Therefore, it is fundamentally aligned with the goals of nursing to facilitate humanization, dignity, choice, quality of life, and healing for persons coping with illness. TREATING PAIN AND OUD Mr. Wright continues 24 mg/day sublingual buprenorphine while following harm reduction recommendations, including carrying naloxone and never using substances when he is alone. Overall, Mr. Wright’s substance use has declined over six months. He says that, despite his cancer, his quality of life is much better than before the diagnosis. Unfortunately, a year after he starts treatment, the pain in his back worsens. Magnetic resonance imaging shows spinal cord compression and several other areas of bone metastasis. He undergoes radiation treatment but continues to have issues with severe pain and loss of function. For the person with pain and comorbid OUD treated with MOUD, the most important consideration is balancing the need for pain control with attending to the OUD. Suppose the individual has pain due to cancer and is currently receiving buprenorphine or methadone to treat OUD. In that case, a first step may be to treat the pain with additional or divided doses of buprenorphine or methadone and use non-opioid analgesics that target the pain etiology. The “7P” framework can be useful in stratifying opioid benefits and harms. (See . ) Although not empirically tested, the 7P framework can assist clinicians in engaging patients in shared decision-making. COPRESCRIBING ANALGESIA Mr. Wright is already taking 24 mg/day of buprenorphine in divided doses. Although the dose of buprenorphine could be increased to the Food and Drug Administration–approved maximum of 32 mg/day, his palliative care clinician decided to add a full opioid agonist instead. Buprenorphine should be continued in people with OUD who are not in sustained recovery (they have had less than three months of MOUD and have continued intermittent substance use). Continuing buprenorphine is often necessary to treat OUD and is preferred to switching to a traditional full agonist only (such as long-acting morphine). , Although this approach has not been well studied in the palliative care literature, the postoperative literature suggest that continuing buprenorphine–naloxone and adding a full opioid agonist is safe and effective for pain. This strategy allows for optimizing treatment of OUD and improving the safety of treating pain with full-agonist opioids. In people with advanced cancer, expert panel consensus also supports continuing buprenorphine for OUD and adding hydromorphone or another short-acting full-agonist opioid to treat pain associated with disease progression. For patients treated with methadone, close collaboration with the opioid treatment program is required. For stable patients, such as people in sustained recovery, take-home weekly doses of methadone (that can also be divided) may be an option in combination with short-acting full agonists for acute pain. Anecdotally, some palliative care practices will take over methadone prescribing in people with serious illness associated with pain and OUD. , This approach should be considered carefully because, unless the prescribing indication is pain, it violates federal policy that stipulates methadone cannot be prescribed for OUD outside of an opioid treatment program. MAINTAINING OUD TREATMENT Mr. Wright has completed radiation treatment for spinal cord compression. His pain is well controlled but he continues to lose weight and spends nearly all of his time in bed or sleeping. He is approaching the end of his life but is unable to remain at home for hospice care. The clinic nurse supporting the palliative care NP attempts to facilitate an inpatient hospice admission, but many facilities are declining him because of their unfamiliarity with buprenorphine. In our clinical experience, as well as in the literature, there are challenges to finding skilled nursing care or hospice placement for people with treated or untreated OUD. Despite the safeguards of the Americans with Disabilities Act, discrimination continues to be an issue, with nearly 40% of people hospitalized for OUD declined skilled nursing care because of their condition or medication. Overt discrimination is partly due to stigma and policy-related barriers. Additionally, many hospices report a lack of familiarity with the comanagement of pain and OUD. Nursing facilities may lack expertise in treating OUD and administering MOUD; they perceive that required care is beyond their skill set and may increase liability. These factors underscore the importance of education on substance use disorder for all clinicians. Future advocacy efforts are needed to address policy-related barriers. In the meantime, nurses in various roles and settings can facilitate proper treatment by coordinating continuing MOUD with existing buprenorphine prescribers or opioid treatment programs. of pain and OUD. Nursing facilities may lack expertise in treating OUD and administering MOUD; they perceive that required care is beyond their skill set and may increase liability. These factors underscore the importance of education on substance use disorder for all clinicians. Future advocacy efforts are needed to address policy-related barriers. In the meantime, nurses in various roles and settings can facilitate proper treatment by coordinating continuing MOUD with existing buprenorphine prescribers or opioid treatment programs. DEATH WITH DIGNITY Because of the clinic nurse’s advocacy, Mr. Wright was accepted to a skilled nursing facility, and he continued to take buprenorphine in the days preceding his death. He told his nurses that he had always feared dying alone of an opioid overdose. Managing his addiction gave him meaning and purpose, allowing him to make peace with himself before he died. Treatment of pain in people with OUD and cancer may feel challenging to clinicians because of their lack of knowledge in this area and their fears and unconscious biases. However, due to the increased recognition of the prevalence of substance use disorder in individuals with a painful serious illness such as cancer, nurses must possess the skills in motivational interviewing, harm reduction, and knowledge of optimal pain treatment and OUD to best meet the needs of this patient population. ▼

documents.title: SCCM Nutrition Therapy Guideline for Adult Critically Ill Patients

chunks.content: Introduction The questions of how much, how soon and by which route to provide nutrition to the critically ill patient have plagued practitioners for decades. As our understanding of the metabolic response to critical illness continues to evolve, our delivery of nutrition therapy has become more nuanced. We are now progressing beyond the one-size-fits-all era into the personalized medicine era of critical care nutrition. Professional societies such as the Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM), American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition (ASPEN), European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) and the Canadian Critical Care network have historically provided recommendations that have been, at times, contradictory. Over time, these recommendations have been converging on alignment for timing of initiation, preferred route and amount of energy (calories) and protein to prescribe. Both underfeeding and overfeeding have recognized harms, and the challenge facing the intensivist is to navigate between Scylla and Charybdis to provide the right dose at the right time by the right route to the right patient. Phases of critical illness In 1942, Cuthbertson first described the ‘ebb’ and ‘flow’ phases of shock followed by a prolonged convalescence phase ( ). For over 50 years, this mental model influenced critical care nutrition. However, improving scientific methods have evolved our understanding of metabolic changes throughout the course of critical illness and our modern model now subdivides the acute phase into early (day 1–2) and late (day 3–7) periods, with an addition of a chronic illness phase (day 7—months) and recognizes that the protracted convalescent recovery phase is often characterized by even higher metabolic requirements ( ). At present, we do not have a reliable bedside means of discerning when the patient progresses from one phase to the next and the time durations about are only rough estimates. It is well-established that critically ill patients experience increased protein degradation and the catabolism (delightfully coined ‘septic autocannibalism’ ) results in a skeletal muscle loss of approximately 2% per day . In the past, intensive care unit (ICU) nutrition strategy was aimed at providing 100% (or greater) of estimated energy requirements in the early stages of critical illness to mitigate catabolism. It is now understood that during the early acute phase of critical illness, multiple metabolic processes such as glycogenolysis, lipolysis and proteolysis all converge with the ultimate goal of endogenous glucose production (EGP). Unfortunately, it is not currently possible to measure the extent of EGP, nor precisely identify when it abates, though it is generally believed to resolve by the end of the first week of critical illness. Importantly, no amount of exogenously provided nutrition can abolish or diminish EGP . Furthermore, isotope studies have shown that whole body protein catabolism continues unabated irrespective of exogenous nutrition. Providing excessive macronutrients during the early acute phase can also lead to other detrimental adverse effects such as accumulation of excess nitrogenous waste products, lipid accumulation causing hepatic steatosis, autophagy suppression (ie, inflammatory priming) and CO 2 overproduction, leading to hypercapnia. For all these reasons, it is no longer recommended to deliver 100% of calories and protein in the first few days of critical illness. Beyond the early acute phase, metabolic requirements generally increase (the traditional ‘flow’ phase) and can last for weeks to months. The existence of the different metabolic phases of critical illness was acknowledged for the first time in the 2019 ESPEN guidelines and the modern ICU nutrition strategy seeks to avoid overfeeding in the early acute phase of critical illness and avoid underfeeding thereafter . Initiation of nutrition therapy With the recognition that EGP will provide a substantial proportion of energy in the early acute phase, and that the patient will likely be receiving additional energy from non-nutritional infusions such as dextrose-containing carrier fluids for medications and propofol (1.1 kcal/mL), both ASPEN and ESPEN both recommend to wait until acute resuscitation (from hemorrhage or distributive shock) is complete before initiating enteral nutrition (EN) or parenteral nutrition (PN). Note that vasopressor infusions are not an absolute contraindication for initiating trophic (‘trickle’) rate (10–20 mL/hour) EN, though most experienced practitioners will wait until the lactic acidosis is improving or stabilized. Unless a contraindication to EN exists (such as bowel discontinuity or obstruction), it is usually feasible to initiate trophic rate EN within 48 hours of ICU admission. Energy assessment ASPEN, ESPEN and the Canadian guidelines all recommend indirect calorimetry (IC) to measure energy expenditure (EE), but they also recognize that access to IC is rare. Therefore, ASPEN and ESPEN provide recommendations to use simplistic weight-based equations (such as 25–30 kcal/kg) or predictive equations (such as Harris-Benedict or Mifflin St. Jeor) if IC is not available. is usually feasible to initiate trophic rate EN within 48 hours of ICU admission. Energy assessment ASPEN, ESPEN and the Canadian guidelines all recommend indirect calorimetry (IC) to measure energy expenditure (EE), but they also recognize that access to IC is rare. Therefore, ASPEN and ESPEN provide recommendations to use simplistic weight-based equations (such as 25–30 kcal/kg) or predictive equations (such as Harris-Benedict or Mifflin St. Jeor) if IC is not available. Two Swiss randomized controlled trials (RCTs), SPN1 and SPN2, have been conducted demonstrating that personalized energy prescription based on IC measurements on ICU day 4 (presumably after the early acute phase) resulted in lower rates of nosocomial infection and less muscle loss. Other investigators have demonstrated longitudinal intrapatient variability in EE throughout the hospital course. If you have access to indirect calorimetry, you should perform your measurements no sooner than ICU day 4 and you should periodically repeat measurements throughout the ICU and hospital course . How much energy to prescribe? Multiple high-quality landmark ICU nutrition RCTs have been published in the past 20 years which have been more informative of actions to avoid, rather than actions that should be taken to optimize the care of the patient. The first wave of these modern landmark studies focused on comparing ‘full’ nutrition versus trophic or permissive underfeeding. Full nutrition is defined as 100% of the kcal or energy requirements as measured by indirect calorimetry or calculated using a weight-based equation (ex: 25–30 kcal/kg) or a predictive equation (such as Harris Benedict or Mifflin-St. Jeor). Two trials (EDEN and PermiT ) both demonstrated no benefit of a strategy of trophic or permissive underfeeding over full feeding ( ). Note that both trials focused on nutrition interventions in the first week of critical illness during the early acute phase when EGP is maximal and full feeding is expected to result in overfeeding. These two trials form the foundation for the ASPEN 2022 guidelines recommendation suggesting ‘feeding between 12 and 25 kcal/kg… in the first 7–10 days of ICU stay’ and the ESPEN 2023 guidelines recommend that ‘hypocaloric nutrition (not exceeding 70% of EE) should be administered in the early phase of acute illness.’ The 2023 NUTRIREA-3 trial randomized 3044 patients enrolled from 61 French ICUs to either low calorie and protein targets (6 kcal/kg/day and 0.2–0.4 g/kg/day) or standard calorie and protein targets (25 kcal/kg/day and 1.0–1.3 g/kg/day) for the first 7 ICU days. Although there was no difference between groups in mortality at 90 days or median time to readiness for ICU discharge, the standard calorie/protein group had significantly higher rates of vomiting, diarrhea and mesenteric ischemia. Stated another way, a Bayesian reanalysis of the NUTRIREA-3 data concluded that the low-energy, low-protein group had an 80% posterior probability of benefit. With these three trials ( ), it is strongly recommended that in order to avoid overfeeding, the energy ‘goal’ should be between 70% and 80%of full nutrition during the early acute phase or for the first week of critical illness. Note that if the patient rapidly improves (ie, weans off vasopressors and is extubated), they are likely no longer in the early acute phase. Beyond the early acute phase and beyond the first week of critical illness, there is very little high-quality evidence that provides guidance, though experts recommend increasing to full nutrition and consider prescribing even higher amounts in the post-ICU phase. ESPEN 2023 guidelines recommend that after day three, energy delivery can be increased up to 80–100% of measured energy expenditure and … isocaloric nutrition rather than hypocaloric nutrition can be progressively implemented after the early phase of acute illness. Protein For nearly the first half-century of critical care, clinicians focused exclusively on debating the dose of energy (calories) to be delivered, with little attention paid to protein delivery. Until the introduction of modular protein supplements in the early 2000s, enteral protein could only be provided as a fixed component of the EN formula. Starting at the turn of the 21st century, though, increasing flexibility in adjusting protein delivery (separate from tube feeds) combined with multiple observational studies reporting lower mortality associated with higher protein delivery, resulted in well-intentioned expert recommendations to prescribe escalating doses of protein to attempt to mitigate catabolism and skeletal muscle loss. Older versions of SCCM/ASPEN guidelines recommended 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day protein based on mostly observational study data. However, small studies suggested the presence of anabolic resistance (ie, inability to utilize exogenous protein/amino acids for the purposes of muscle protein synthesis). Three recent landmark trials have provided high-level evidence to reduce the enthusiasm for high-protein delivery in the early acute phase of critical illness. The EFFORT Protein trial randomized 1301 patients from 85 international ICUs to either high-dose protein (≥2.2 g/kg/day) or usual dose protein (≤1.2 g/kg/day) within 96 hours of ICU admission and continued

attempt to mitigate catabolism and skeletal muscle loss. Older versions of SCCM/ASPEN guidelines recommended 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day protein based on mostly observational study data. However, small studies suggested the presence of anabolic resistance (ie, inability to utilize exogenous protein/amino acids for the purposes of muscle protein synthesis). Three recent landmark trials have provided high-level evidence to reduce the enthusiasm for high-protein delivery in the early acute phase of critical illness. The EFFORT Protein trial randomized 1301 patients from 85 international ICUs to either high-dose protein (≥2.2 g/kg/day) or usual dose protein (≤1.2 g/kg/day) within 96 hours of ICU admission and continued for up to 28 days, death or transition to oral intake. The primary endpoint of cumulative incidence of alive hospital discharge at 60 days was 46.1% in the high-dose group compared with 50.2% in the usual dose group. In the subgroup of patients with acute kidney injury not receiving continuous renal replacement therapy with high organ failure scores, mortality was higher in the high-dose group. Stated another way, a Bayesian reanalysis of the data concluded that the high-dose protein group had an 80% posterior probability of harm. The TARGET Protein trial randomized 3397 patients enrolled from 8 ICUs across Australia and New Zealand to either usual protein formula (63 g protein/L) or augmented protein (100 g protein/L) in a cluster randomized, cross-over fashion. Subjects in both groups received equivalent amounts of energy and fluids. There was no difference between groups in the primary endpoint of hospital-free and alive at day 90, nor were there any differences in survival, quality of life or functional outcomes at 6 months. The PRECISe trial randomized 935 patients enrolled from 10 ICUs in the Netherlands and Belgium to either standard protein formula or high protein formula. Subjects received their assigned formula for the entire duration of EN in the ICU up to 90 days. The primary outcome of EuroQoL 5-Dimension 5-level (a validated measure of patient-reported functional status and quality of life) at 180 days was lower in patients assigned to the high protein formula. Additionally, the high-protein formula group had a higher incidence of gastrointestinal (GI) intolerance. Stated another way, the posterior probability of benefit from high protein targets with respect to the EQ-5D-5L health utility score was 0% and the posterior probability of clinically important harm was 47%. A Bayesian meta-analysis of all 22 trials up through September 2024 (including EFFORT and PRECISe) concluded a 56% posterior probability of harm, resulting from higher protein delivery. With the EFFORT, TARGET and PRECISe trials showing no benefit and potential harm resulting from early, high-protein delivery ( ), the ESPEN 2023 guidelines recommend ‘1.3 g/kg protein equivalents per day’. The ASPEN 2022 guidelines were published prior to the publication of the EFFORT and PRECISe trials. Based on the recent large high-quality randomized trials, it is recommended to provide no more than 1.2 g/kg/day protein in the early acute phase of critical illness. As with calorie prescription, there is a relative dearth of high-quality literature to guide protein prescription beyond the first week of ICU, but experts currently recommend increasing protein prescription to 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day in the chronic and post-ICU phase and even higher to 2.0 to 2.5 g/kg/g after hospital discharge. Supplementation via EN or PN may be necessary, as energy and protein intake have been shown to be woefully inadequate after ICU discharge, especially in patients relying solely on oral intake. Enteral versus parenteral When a patient is eligible for both EN and PN, the clinician must carefully weigh the advantages and disadvantages of each mode of delivery. On the one hand, EN is more physiologic, cost-effective and has additional non-nutritional benefits (such as maintaining mucosal integrity); however, the amount of EN formula actually absorbed by the gastrointestinal tract (GI) is unknown and the rate of GI dysfunction is very high, especially in surgical and trauma patients. Complications such as aspiration and mesenteric ischemia can be fatal. Although it is generally accepted that small bowel (post-pyloric) feeding is associated with reduced rates of pneumonia and improved calorie and protein delivery, the difficulty in obtaining postpyloric access and associated delay in initiating EN can negate those benefits. Therefore, both ASPEN/SCCM and ESPEN recommend (based on expert consensus) that is acceptable to begin with gastric EN in the majority of critically ill patients. However, in patients with high risk for aspiration or for those who have already demonstrated signs and symptoms of GI intolerance, postpyloric feeding is recommended. This access may be accomplished by blind insertion at bedside or through the use of magnetic or optical bedside insertion techniques or with the help of endoscopy or fluoroscopy. PN has the advantage of providing a known amount of nutrition directly into the blood stream and allows more customization options regarding energy/protein/micronutrients, but requires central venous access, can result

However, in patients with high risk for aspiration or for those who have already demonstrated signs and symptoms of GI intolerance, postpyloric feeding is recommended. This access may be accomplished by blind insertion at bedside or through the use of magnetic or optical bedside insertion techniques or with the help of endoscopy or fluoroscopy. PN has the advantage of providing a known amount of nutrition directly into the blood stream and allows more customization options regarding energy/protein/micronutrients, but requires central venous access, can result in infectious and metabolic complications and delivers the nutrients in a very non-physiologic manner. The early decades of PN (1970s–1990s) were marked by exuberant overfeeding (‘hyperalimentation’), lax glycemic control and soy-based (pro-inflammatory Ω −6) lipid injectable emulsions. It is thus not surprising that infection rates up to 90% were reported and some have referred to TPN as ‘total poisonous nutrition.’ The 1990s saw a backlash against PN and the beginning of an era of advocating for EN as the preferred mode of nutrition delivery. Advancements in critical care and nutrition in the decades that followed include tight glycemic control, restrictive blood transfusion, fluid restriction, lung-protective ventilation, catheter care bundles and the introduction of mixed lipid emulsions containing anti-inflammatory (Ω −3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, PUFAs ) fish oil. Additionally, with the recognition of the harms of overfeeding, the era of ‘hyperalimentation’ officially ended. The modern 21st century PN has become a lot safer and multiple high-quality RCTs have demonstrated infection rates equivalent to EN, with one exception ( ). The notable deviation is the 2011 EPaNIC trial, which compared early to late PN. It is important to note, though, that the EPaNIC trial enrolled mostly low-acuity, well-nourished cardiac surgery patients. Furthermore, subjects randomized to early PN received an infusion of intravenous 20% glucose solution for the first two ICU days, with full (100%) PN starting on ICU day 3. Thus, this trial study cohort and practices limit the generalizability of its conclusions. After decades of recommending EN over PN, the 2022 ASPEN updated guidelines state that … no differences in harm were identified, we recommend that either PN or EN is acceptable . Similarly, the 2018 Canadian Critical Care Nutrition guidelines conclude that EN is not associated with improvements in survival, hospital length of stay or caloric delivery but may be associated with increased episodes of vomiting. However, PN remains more costly and lacks the non-nutritive benefits (regarding mucosal integrity, bacterial translocation, motility, microbiome and hormonal/metabolic signaling ) that EN can provide. For those patients with absolute contraindications to EN, the decision to begin PN within the first week of critical illness depends on the baseline nutritional status. It is estimated that up to 40% of ICU patients have some degree of malnutrition at admission and these patients may not have sufficient reserves (glycogen, adipose tissue and skeletal muscle) for EGP. The ESPEN V.2023 guidelines recommend that early and progressive PN can be provided in lieu of withholding nutrition in the setting of EN contraindications in severely malnourished patients . Exercise and neuromuscular electrical stimulation Finally, it has been suggested that nutrition, to borrow a legal term, may be necessary but not sufficient . Approximately 40% of ICU survivors experience ICU-acquired weakness and one potential reason why ICU nutrition studies have failed to demonstrate superiority of higher energy and protein delivery may be the lack of accompanying physical therapy (PT) to use the nutrient substrates to build muscle. Studies in healthy adults have shown that exercise enhances muscle protein synthesis using dietary protein-derived amino acids. Accumulating evidence demonstrates that early and aggressive PT is feasible and beneficial, even in the early acute phase of critical illness when patients are intubated and receiving vasopressors. Multiple randomized trials have concluded that combining nutrition and exercise early in the course of critical illness has beneficial clinical outcomes while trials investigating only PT (without high-protein) have not shown benefit. For patients unable to participate in PT, muscle contraction via electrical stimulation has been shown to preserve muscle strength and prevent muscle atrophy. Immunonutrition Surgical trauma and critical illness both trigger a complex inflammatory cascade that can profoundly affect the clinical course. ‘Immunonutrition’ refers to the strategic use of nutrients at supraphysiologic pharmacologic doses to modulate the immune response to stress. Specially formulated EN formulas containing arginine, glutamine, nucleotides and Ω −3 PUFAs became available in the 1990s and a wave of enthusiasm followed. Numerous RCTs were conducted, but heterogeneity in formula content, dose, duration, patient population and outcomes continue to plague the literature and preclude strong recommendations. Additionally, selective reporting, publication bias and industry bias also confound the interpretation of the literature. Glutamine The amino acid glutamine is involved in multiple physiologic regulatory pathways, including

can profoundly affect the clinical course. ‘Immunonutrition’ refers to the strategic use of nutrients at supraphysiologic pharmacologic doses to modulate the immune response to stress. Specially formulated EN formulas containing arginine, glutamine, nucleotides and Ω −3 PUFAs became available in the 1990s and a wave of enthusiasm followed. Numerous RCTs were conducted, but heterogeneity in formula content, dose, duration, patient population and outcomes continue to plague the literature and preclude strong recommendations. Additionally, selective reporting, publication bias and industry bias also confound the interpretation of the literature. Glutamine The amino acid glutamine is involved in multiple physiologic regulatory pathways, including acid-base, nitrogen transport, immune cell proliferation, neutrophil function and antioxidant defense. In previous guideline iterations, intravenous glutamine was routinely recommended by ASPEN and ESPEN. However, the publication of two high-quality RCTs in 2013 and 2014 abruptly changed practice. The REDOX trial randomly assigned 1223 patients from 40 ICUs across the USA, Canada and Europe to receive supplements of glutamine, antioxidants, both or placebo in a 2×2 factorial design. There was no benefit in those subjects that received glutamine and instead there was a trend towards higher mortality, particularly those with multiorgan failure. Antioxidants were neither beneficial nor harmful. The following year, the MetaPlus trial randomly assigned 301 patients enrolled from 14 ICUs in Europe to receive a high-protein enteral formula enriched with immunonutrients or a standard high-protein formula (without immunonutrients). No difference in the primary outcome of new infections was observed and there was a signal towards higher 6-month mortality in the medical subgroup of patients. After REDOX and MetaPlus, a third trial (GLND) was published in 2016. GLND enrolled exclusively postoperative surgical patients expected to require PN for at least 7 days and randomized subjects to receive either PN containing alanyl-glutamine at a dose of 0.5 g/kg/day or a conventional glutamine-free PN formula containing standard amino acid formula for up to 28 days. Importantly, the GLND trial excluded patients with hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressor support and significant renal dysfunction. Although no significant differences were observed in the primary outcomes of hospital mortality and new total hospital-acquired infections, there were also no significant differences in adverse events or other signals of harm. With the publication of this trio of trials, the use of intravenous glutamine and antioxidants abruptly stopped in the vast majority of ICU patients. Enteral glutamine continued to be prescribed to burn patients until the publication of the 2022 RE-ENERGIZE trial. In this large trial, 1209 patients with severe burns (mean 33% TBSA) were randomly assigned to receive either enterally delivered glutamine or placebo. As with REDOX, no significant difference was observed in 6 month mortality or time to discharge alive from the hospital. Based on these high-quality trials (REDOX, MetaPlus, GLND, and RE-ENERGIZE) ( ), at present, glutamine (IV or EN) as a sole immunonutrient is no longer recommended in critically ill patients, though it continues to be delivered as part of a multi-component bundle including other immunonutrients in commercial formulas . Arginine Arginine stimulates lymphocyte proliferation, enhances macrophage function and is essential for T-cell and neutrophil function. There are several plausible mechanistic benefits of arginine supplementation in critically ill patients, though clinical evidence is mixed and the 2016 ASPEN guidelines provide only weak recommendations for supplementation of arginine-containing enteral formulas in critically ill trauma and brain injured patients, though they are NOT recommended in medical or sepsis patients . The differential responses between these cohorts likely reflect fundamental differences in arginine metabolism and the inflammatory milieu. Fish oil (Ω −3 PUFAs) Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) exert anti-inflammatory effects through multiple inter-related pathways. For example, EPA and DHA incorporate into cellular membrane phospholipids, displacing arachidonic acid and shifting eicosanoid production from highly pro-inflammatory mediators (PGE2 = prostaglandin E2, TXA₂= trhomboxane A2, LTB₄= leukotriene B4) to less inflammatory mediators (PGE₃, TXA₃, LTB₅). Additionally, EPA and DHA serve as precursors for specialized pro-resolving mediators (including resolvins, protectins and maresins) that reduce neutrophil infiltration and enhance macrophage-mediated debris clearance. They also enhance transcriptional reprogramming to decrease expression of multiple cytokines and adhesion molecules. From 1975 to 2016, the only lipid injectable emulsion available to patients in the USA was 100% soy-based, containing pro-inflammatory Ω −6 fatty acids. In 2016, the Food and Drug Administration approved a mixed-lipid emulsion containing fish oil (anti-inflammatory Ω−3 PUFAs), though it had been available in Europe since 2004. Recognizing the pro-inflammatory nature of soy-based lipids, earlier versions of the ASPEN guidelines specifically recommended that ‘in the first week of hospitalization in the ICU, when PN is required and EN is not feasible, patients should be given a parenteral formulation without soy-based lipids (2009)’ and ‘suggest withholding or limiting soybean oil-based intravenous fat emulsions during the first week (2016)’. However, the 2022 ASPEN guidelines now state that either mixed-oil lipid injectable emulsions or

In 2016, the Food and Drug Administration approved a mixed-lipid emulsion containing fish oil (anti-inflammatory Ω−3 PUFAs), though it had been available in Europe since 2004. Recognizing the pro-inflammatory nature of soy-based lipids, earlier versions of the ASPEN guidelines specifically recommended that ‘in the first week of hospitalization in the ICU, when PN is required and EN is not feasible, patients should be given a parenteral formulation without soy-based lipids (2009)’ and ‘suggest withholding or limiting soybean oil-based intravenous fat emulsions during the first week (2016)’. However, the 2022 ASPEN guidelines now state that either mixed-oil lipid injectable emulsions or 100% soybean-oil lipid injectable emulsions be provided to critically ill patients who are appropriate candidates for initiation of PN, including within the first week of ICU admission … and the ESPEN 2023 guidelines recommend that parenteral lipid emulsions enriched with EPA and DHA can be provided in patients receiving PN . Future studies will answer the question of whether or not intravenous fish oil separate from PN indications can provide clinical benefit. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) and B<sub>1</sub> (thiamine) In 2017, Marik et al published a highly influential publication reporting incredible improvements in mortality (8.5% vs 40.4%) associated with a cocktail containing hydrocortisone, ascorbic acid and thiamine, the so-called ‘metabolic resuscitation’ Marik cocktail. This study stimulated a period of intense research in the ensuing years. Unfortunately, subsequent multicenter RCTs failed to replicate these findings and instead reported increased mortality with high-dose ascorbic acid and the metabolic resuscitation bundles. In less than 8 years, the use of empiric high-dose ascorbic acid and thiamine swung from rarely used, to highly popular, and back to rarely used. Although the latest ASPEN and ESPEN guidelines do not specifically recommend for or against ascorbic acid or thiamine, empiric use of these micronutrients has fallen out of favor and are rarely, if ever, used in modern clinical practice. Other immunonutrients Other immunonutrients such as branched-chain amino acids and other nucleotides and antioxidants such as vitamin A (retinol), vitamin E (tocopherol), vitamin B 12 (cyanocobalamin) and selenium lack sufficient evidence to recommend for or against their empiric use beyond specific clinical deficiencies. Summary of immunonutrition literature Three decades of intense research have produced a confusing corpus of heterogeneous and conflicting trials plagued by multiple methodological flaws precluding adequate analysis of the individual components of immunonutrition. However, recent high-quality RCTs have diminished enthusiasm for intravenous glutamine in all ICU patients and enteral glutamine in severe burn patients. Arginine is not recommended as a standalone immunonutrition but is weakly recommended as a part of a multicomponent enteral supplement in select ICU populations, namely trauma and brain-injured patients. The most promising immunonutrient is fish oil (Ω −3 PUFAs), which has anti-inflammatory properties and has been shown to be safe and likely beneficial in the first week of critical illness. Conclusions Recommendations for evidence-based ICU nutrition are summarized in . In the absence of contraindications to EN, trophic rate EN should begin when acute resuscitation is complete, typically within 48 hours of ICU admission. During the first week or early acute phase of critical illness, energy delivery should be limited to no more than 70%–80% of ‘full’ nutrition because of the unavoidable presence of EGP. Similarly, protein delivery should be limited to ≤1.2 g/kg/day. After the early acute phase, both energy and protein prescription should increase to 100% ‘full’ nutrition and 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day. In the chronic convalescent and post-ICU phase, even higher energy and protein prescriptions may be necessary to regain lost muscle mass and function. Early PT or neuromuscular stimulation is safe, feasible and likely beneficial. Although intravenous glutamine and arginine are no longer recommended, there may be a role for intravenous fish oil and enteral glutamine (only for burns >20% TBSA).

chunks.content: Introduction In 2010, twelve German medical societies published the Evidence- and Consensus-based Guidelines on the Management of Analgesia, Sedation and Delirium . Since this publication, the body of evidence in the field has increased considerably. Several new studies and publications, including the new recommendations from the American College of Critical Care Medicine (ACCM) in conjunction with Society of Critical Care Medicine (SCCM) and American Society of Health-System Pharmacists (ASHP) in 2013, make a substantial actualization of the German guidelines necessary. This update not only accounts for new evidence, but also contains a major restructuring and extension of the guidelines to cover new aspects of treatment, such as sleep and anxiety management. This new version aims to provide practical guidance for the symptom-based prevention, diagnostics and therapy of delirium, anxiety, and agitation, as well as for the protocol-based analgesia, sedation, and sleep management during critical illness. Under the guidance of the German Society of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Care Medicine (DGAI) and German Interdisciplinary Association for Intensive Care and Emergency Medicine (DIVI), this is one of the most comprehensive guidelines worldwide, being developed and approved by 17 national societies. These guidelines were developed for all professions working in the intensive care unit (ICU), and its recommendations encompass critically ill patients of all age groups and severity of illness, regardless of comorbidities. Delirium and coma are the most common manifestations of acute brain dysfunction during critical illness. Pain, stress, and a disruption of the sleep-wake-cycle are typical symptoms observed during ICU treatment, all of which can lead to delirium and impair outcome. An early management of these symptoms improves recovery and long-term outcome, while reducing post-intensive-care-unit-syndrome (PICS) and mortality. The basic principle follows an “early goal directed therapy” (EGDT) with immediate and evidence-based targets for treatment, the assessment of the clinical situation with validated instruments, and the goal-directed pharmacological therapy. These measures are to be accompanied by non-pharmacological interventions aimed at prevention and treatment. The critically ill patient should be awake and alert, without pain, anxiety, or delirium. Ultimately, this allows the patient to actively participate in their treatment and recovery. The term “sedation” was left in the title intentionally: the indication and conduction of sedation require special attention in order not to harm the patient through oversedation, as this has been proven to negatively affect patient outcome. In the interest of the patients, the use of sedatives and analgesics must therefore be very carefully considered. The patient must be allowed to be as alert and oriented as possible, so that they may partake in the therapy and convalescence process, as evidence shows is feasible, practical, and safe. Methods This guideline has the highest development credentials, S3, indicating that it is both evidence- and consensus based. The guideline task-force consisted of 49 voting members nominated by 17 participating national societies. These members formed work groups that identified main clinical issues and framed key-questions to be addressed. Should previous versions of the guideline not /no longer provide satisfactory resolutions to the selected topics, search strategies were developed to address the subject. The resulting recommendations were then collected in an early version and further discussed within the groups. The members interacted with each other via consensus-conferences, email, fax, or mail. Communication was managed by a coordinating group consisting of 4 members, as well as the chairing societies. A systematic literature search was performed by a special team under the supervision of an epidemiologist. Finally, the evaluation process was done by the individual working groups, which also set the level-of-evidence (LoE). All searches were performed between April and May of 2014. When necessary, new evidence was integrated manually. The LoE was determined, as in the previous version of the guideline, using the Oxford System [ ]. The overview tables allow to identification the evidence for each individual manuscript. Literature was accessible for all task-force members. The specific search strategies, searched terms, inclusion and exclusion criteria, as well as exact time frames, are all detailed in the methodological report. Sources were electronic databases (Medline ® ), guideline networks, and (manually) abstracts and congress-publications. In order to identify “grey literature”, all task-force members were asked to search for publications outside Medline and Embase and include relevant entries to the literature-data-base. Systematic guideline searches were conducted within the AWMF-registry ( http://www.awmf.org/leitlinien.html ) and the Guidelines International Network (G-I-N) ( http://www.g-i-n.net ). In line with the AWMF-guideline developer manual, a consensus-based decision was used to assess whether recommendations from other guidelines could be adapted. Cultural adaptions were adopted in accordance with recommendations from the ADAPTE-Collaboration [ ]. Voting only took place following a full disclosure of potential conflicts of interest by the task-force members. The conflict of interest forms were stored centrally, and all task-force members declaring a conflict of interest were required to abstain from voting in the corresponding

In line with the AWMF-guideline developer manual, a consensus-based decision was used to assess whether recommendations from other guidelines could be adapted. Cultural adaptions were adopted in accordance with recommendations from the ADAPTE-Collaboration [ ]. Voting only took place following a full disclosure of potential conflicts of interest by the task-force members. The conflict of interest forms were stored centrally, and all task-force members declaring a conflict of interest were required to abstain from voting in the corresponding issues. This was consented in the task-force before the voting process. The voting-process itself was conducted during consensus-conferences, under the supervision of an independent observer from the AWMF. Alternatively, members could vote using an online DELPHI, as published and recommended in the AWMF-guideline developer manual. The used grades of recommendation (GoR) were A = strong recommendation (we recommend/one shall), B = recommendation (we suggest/one should), and O = open recommendation (one might consider) for or against any specific intervention. Significant deviations between LoE and GoR were generally possible if a member of the group requested upgrading or downgrading of a recommendation (e.g. due to ethical relevance or lack of research-possibilities). Expert opinions and consensus-based decisions were only allowed when the resolutions were highly relevant for clinical routine and there was lack of available evidence. The guideline was reviewed and approved by 17 scientific societies. Reviewers were all independent peers. All procedures are in adherence to the actualization protocol. The next regular update of the guideline is scheduled for 2018, although earlier modifications are permitted should significant new evidence arise. Management of delirium, analgesia, and sedation in adult intensive care Risk and prevention of ICU related delirium Pain, stress, anxiety, and a disrupted sleep-wake cycle are common symptoms that occur in critically ill patients that increase the risk for ICU related delirium [ ]. Delirium is one of the most common manifestations of cerebral dysfunction in critically ill patients, which affects not only short-term recovery (in terms of prolonged ventilation and length of stay, as well as increased mortality) [ ], [ ], [ ], but also leads to cognitive long-term impairment, posttraumatic stress disorders (PTSD), and reduced quality of life [ ]. These entities are part of the Post Intensive Care Unit Syndrome (PICS) that has been recently described in ICU survivors. Aside from managing the risk factors, several effective pharmacological and non-pharmacological prevention strategies can be used to prevent or treat ICU delirium. In addition to baseline factors, the risk for delirium also comprises treatment associated factors, as well as psychological, social, and iatrogenic aspects [ ]. The presence or development of risk factors for delirium shall be closely evaluated in order to ensure the prompt introduction of preventive measures. The non-pharmacological measures were shown to be particularly effective in the prevention of delirium, and shall therefore be implemented for all critically ill patients. The excessive use of sedation shall be avoided, since a deep sedation were shown to deteriorate the clinical outcome [ ]. A pharmacological prevention is to be reserved only for patients at high risk for delirium, and is not generally recommended (Table 1 , Table 2 , Table 3 ). Monitoring of analgesia, sedation, delirium, anxiety, stress, and sleep A basic concept of patient-oriented therapy in intensive-care is the definition of a patient-specific treatment goal, and the frequent assessment of the current status in order to promptly introduce or adjust interventions (Goal Directed Therapy). The definition and monitoring of treatment goals must be symptom-oriented, using validated scores and instruments. The use of such validated methods has a major impact on treatment: the systematic evaluation of pain, sedation, and delirium can significantly improve treatment of pain, reduce nosocomial infections, decrease duration of mechanical ventilation and hospitalization, as well as reduce mortality [ ], [ ]. Therefore, it should be a standard in all ICUs to define goals, measure, and document the current state of analgesia, sedation, and delirium once per shift (usually every 8 hours) with a validated clinical scores and instruments (Figure 1 ). The evaluation of anxiety with a validated scale is desirable, since anxiety is often not properly estimated, and thus not properly treated. There are short versions of standard psychological measurement instruments available (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, state subscale [STAI-s], Brief Symptom Inventory Anxiety, subscale [BSI-A]) that allow a valid and reliable assessment of anxiety. From pain assessment, we know that one-dimensional self-assessment scales have proven to be especially practical to measure therapeutic needs and therapeutic response. From pain assessment studies, it is clear that the use one-dimensional self-assessment scales are particularly useful in evaluating the therapeutic needs and therapeutic response. Studies on anxiety show that similar scales (for example linear Visual Analogue

anxiety is often not properly estimated, and thus not properly treated. There are short versions of standard psychological measurement instruments available (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, state subscale [STAI-s], Brief Symptom Inventory Anxiety, subscale [BSI-A]) that allow a valid and reliable assessment of anxiety. From pain assessment, we know that one-dimensional self-assessment scales have proven to be especially practical to measure therapeutic needs and therapeutic response. From pain assessment studies, it is clear that the use one-dimensional self-assessment scales are particularly useful in evaluating the therapeutic needs and therapeutic response. Studies on anxiety show that similar scales (for example linear Visual Analogue Scale and the Faces Anxiety Scale) are also suitable to measure anxiety with good diagnostic validity [ ]. Further studies are needed to clarify whether the controllability of anxiolysis can also be monitored with these scales. Stress and disturbances of the sleep-wake cycle are further syndromes in ICU-patients that not only negatively affect recovery, but also constitute risk factors for serious complications. Nevertheless, there are currently no validated routine instrument for measuring stress and sleep, and the sole subjective assessment of vital signs by the ICU personnel is not suitable to monitor stress in critically ill patients [ ]. Regarding the sleep-wake cycle of ICU patients, not only is there a lack of suitable monitoring procedures that can be routinely used, but also no valid evaluation of sleep stages in critically ill subjects [ ] (Table 4 , Table 5 , Table 6 , Table 7 , Table 8 , Table 9 ). Treatment concepts See Figure 2 . Non-pharmacological concepts See Table 10 . Analgesia ICU-patients require an individualized pain management. Pain exerts considerable negative effects on recovery and is one of the most commonly reported stressors for ICU-patients. Therefore, a sufficient analgesia in all ICU patients – regardless of indication of sedation – should be ensured, and potentially painful procedures should be met with a preventive analgesic approach. In the ICU, the analgesia regimen is usually opioid based [ ], [ ], [ ], [ ], as the risk-benefit profile of non-opioid analgesics is still a matter of scientific discussion (low analgesic potential, but considerable side effects). A combination with regional analgesia can be used [ ], and a patient-controlled analgesia is recommended as soon as the patient is sufficiently awake (RASS 0/-1 and no delirium) [ ] (Table 11 ). Sedation The current evidence reveals that a measurable sedation should always be avoided, as long as there is no mandatory clinical indication for sedation [ ], [ ]. A deep sedation, also within the first 48 hours, is associated with increased mortality, prolonged mechanical ventilation, prolonged ICU-LOS, and hospitalization [ ], [ ], [ ], [ ]. Aside from specific indications (e.g. surgical indications, signs of increased intracranial pressure with impending herniation, or reduction of oxygen consumption in case of imminent hypoxia), the treatment goal should be an alert, cooperative patient who can tolerate the required interventions (RASS 0/–1). It is fundamental to achieve an adequate analgesia, which is accompanied by a specific treatment of possible symptoms, such as hallucinations, stress, and anxiety [ ], [ ], [ ]. A recent systematic review revealed a decreased importance of daily sedation interruptions (DSIs), which is no longer considered superior to protocol-driven management of sedation [ ]. The goal for light sedation should be set as early as possible, as the first 48 hours of sedation predict long-term outcome. Sedation should follow the principles of an “early goal directed therapy” with target-RASS 0/–1 (Table 12 ). Moderate or deep sedation If the indication for a deep sedation is provided, the target RASS and the time of the next re-evaluation must be defined. Sedation should be performed with a combination of hypnotic and analgesic agents, whereas the choice of hypnotic agent should be appropriate to level of sedation and controllability desired. Aside from propofol and benzodiazepines, volatile anesthetics are also feasible options. In the absence of contraindications, DSI protocol (e.g., Spontaneous Awakening Trial, SAT) and Spontaneous Breathing Trials (SBT) should be carried out daily in patients with RASS ≤–2 [ ] (Table 13 ). Symptom oriented sedative therapy Aside from pain, the most common symptoms of critically ill patients are stress, anxiety, agitation, psychotic symptoms, and sleep disturbances, all of which require a targeted, symptom-oriented therapy. In addition to non-pharmacological strategies and a causal treatment, a pharmacological therapy may be necessary to control the symptoms. Alpha-2-agonists are available for stress-reduction and treatment of vegetative symptoms, and benzodiazepines can be used for anxiolysis (Table 14 ). Pharmacological therapy of delirium Preventive measures for delirium are both safe and effective [ ]. If delirium does occur, it should be treated promptly and symptomatically. The treatment of psychotic symptoms (with or without delirium) may include low-dose neuroleptics [ ]. In addition, the use
